# Chapter 7 — Aurielle: "The Real Briefing"nn---

> "A system is not what it does when observed. A system is what it does when the observer has been optimized to look elsewhere."
>
> — *The Cascade Lectures* — Vasht, 2161

---

## Draft v1

Eduardo's chair was too large for her.

Not physically. The ergonomic systems had adjusted within seconds of her first sitting — nanite-threaded leather reshaping itself to her frame, the lumbar support recalibrating, the seat height correcting by two centimeters to bring her eyeline level with the boardroom table. Physically, the chair fit. But the chair had been Eduardo's for eleven years, and the leather still carried the impression of his weight, and every time Aurielle settled into it she felt the architecture of a body that was no longer there.

She hadn't replaced it. She would not replace it. The desk either — Spanish walnut, shipped from Cádiz when Eduardo first took the position, a reminder of where the Vasquez name had started before it became a corporate dynasty. Polished to a depth that held light the way a window holds a view. The surface was clear. Eduardo had kept it clear. She kept it clear. A NitroCore-branded glass of filtered water, positioned on her left within reach. Three datapads, stacked. Nothing else. Empty surfaces projected control. Eduardo's rule, though she couldn't remember him saying it. Some lessons arrived as inheritance rather than instruction — absorbed into posture, into habit, into the precise angle at which she held her shoulders when the boardroom doors opened and fifteen faces turned toward the head of the table.

Toward the Chair. NitroCore's designation for the combined CEO and Board Chair — the position that held both operational authority and governance control. Eduardo had held both. Now she did.

The quarterly board review convened at 09:00 in the NitroCore Executive Chamber — six floors below the Celestial Ballroom where, three weeks ago, the previous occupant of this chair had been holding a lectern while a thermal-kinetic round erased him from the nose up. The Chamber was designed for a different kind of performance. No windows. No external light. The room was a sealed ovoid of dark wood paneling and recessed ambient lighting, temperature-controlled to 21.2 degrees — the precise temperature at which physiological stress responses were minimally activated, according to the behavioral optimization study NitroCore had commissioned in 2168. The table was a single piece of composite, curved to ensure that every seat had sightlines to every other seat and to the holographic display array suspended from the ceiling. The hum of the environmental systems was calibrated to a frequency that the human ear registered as silence.

Aurielle had reviewed the room specifications her second day in the Chair. She reviewed everything. The quarterly projections, the legal exposure summaries, the infrastructure status reports, the personnel reviews, the R&D pipeline, the regional extraction yields, the diplomatic correspondence from the three trade liaison offices, the classified intelligence briefs that arrived on her desk at 06:00 and were collected by a security officer at 07:30 — all of it, every morning, before the first meeting. Eduardo had done the same. She'd learned this not from Eduardo but from his executive assistant, who had mentioned it as a curiosity during the transition briefing: *Your father read everything. Most CEOs delegate the reading. He didn't trust delegation with information.*

She didn't trust it either. That was the inheritance working.

"Good morning." Her voice carried the room without effort — the acoustics were designed for the Chair's position, amplifying slightly from the head of the table. She didn't need to project. The architecture projected for her.

Fifteen faces. She knew them. Director Chen-Nakamura, CFO, seated to her immediate right — the same position she'd held for Eduardo, the same expression of composed institutional support, the same pearl earrings she wore to every formal session as if they were part of a uniform. Beyond her, the divisional heads: Extraction, Refinement, Distribution, Research, Legal, Government Relations. The board liaisons — two external directors whose primary function was to represent shareholder interests and whose secondary function was to report the board's mood back to the investors who had placed them. And at the far end of the curved table, positioned where the sightlines converged but the acoustics slightly diminished — a placement that was either accidental or precisely calculated — Marcus Thorne.

He sat the way he always sat. Hands folded. Expression attentive. The same suit he'd worn at the gala — not the same suit, of course, but the same *kind* of suit, the same cut, the same dark fabric that absorbed light rather than reflecting it. She'd noticed this about Thorne: he dressed to disappear into rooms rather than dominate them. Eduardo had dressed to be seen. Thorne dressed to watch.

His suit had been clean that night. Two chairs away from a thermal-kinetic round and his suit had been *clean.*

She sealed it. The thought went where it always went — into the partition, the compartment she'd built in the three weeks since the gala, the space where the tight jaw lived alongside the steady hands, where the questions about his clean suit coexisted with reliance on his institutional knowledge, neither canceling the other. She sealed it and turned to the agenda.

"Let's begin with the quarterly overview."

---

The numbers were excellent.

Chen-Nakamura walked the board through the Q4 2174 financials with the practiced fluency of someone who had been presenting quarterly numbers for longer than Aurielle had been alive. Revenue up 4.2% year-over-year. Extraction yields stable across all seven primary sites. Refinement efficiency at 98.7% — a record, attributable to the new catalyst formulation the R&D division had deployed in Q3. Distribution network operating at full capacity. Stock price recovered within forty-eight hours of the assassination — a fact Chen-Nakamura presented without inflection, as if the market's response to Eduardo's death were simply another data point in a series of data points, which, from the institution's perspective, it was.

Aurielle listened the way she'd learned to listen in these rooms. Not to the content — she'd read the content already, twice, starting from the last page because that was where the recommendations lived and the recommendations told you what the numbers were supposed to mean. She listened to the delivery. Who paused before which figures. Who glanced at Thorne. Who avoided her eyes and who held them a beat too long, performing loyalty with the same deliberate precision she performed authority.

The room was cooperative. She'd expected resistance — the new CEO, the young CEO, the CEO who'd inherited the position in blood rather than earning it through the decades of institutional climbing that the people in this room had endured. But there was no resistance. The board treated her with the same deference they'd shown Eduardo, and the deference was not performance. It was *institutional*. The Chair commanded it. The person in the Chair was secondary.

This should have been reassuring. It was not.

Slide seventeen.

Chen-Nakamura's voice continued — steady, professional, moving through the divisional breakdowns with the rhythm of someone reading a document she'd written and approved and rehearsed. Extraction Division: within projections. Refinement Division: above projections. Distribution Division: within projections. Research Division: within projections.

Sump Infrastructure Division.

The slide was formatted identically to the others — NitroCore's visual identity was rigorous, every presentation template controlled by the Communications office, every font and color and spacing ratio specified to a degree that bordered on liturgical. The same dark background, the same amber accent lines, the same clean sans-serif type. The title read: *Sump Infrastructure Lifecycle Management — Q4 2174 Summary.*

The numbers beneath it were different from the other divisions. Not worse — different. The metrics were unfamiliar. *Managed attrition rate. Throughput variance by sector. Containment expenditure (deferred).* She knew what each word meant individually. She did not know what they meant together, in this configuration, applied to this division. She did not know what "lifecycle management" meant when the lifecycle in question was infrastructure — or whether it was infrastructure at all.

She didn't ask.

The thought arrived as a small, precise calculation — not a decision but a reading of the room. Fifteen faces, none of them confused. Chen-Nakamura's voice unchanged. Thorne's expression unchanged. The slide was on screen for twelve seconds before Chen-Nakamura advanced to the next divisional summary, and in those twelve seconds Aurielle's mind performed the assessment that Eduardo's training had made reflexive: *Is this a question I can ask without revealing that I don't already know the answer?*

No.

The Chair was supposed to know. Eduardo had known. Eduardo had sat in this seat and reviewed these numbers for eleven years, and the terminology on slide seventeen was part of a vocabulary he had mastered so thoroughly that it required no explanation, and the board members who sat in this room had been briefed on this vocabulary, and the presentation proceeded on the assumption that the person at the head of the table understood what *Sump Infrastructure Lifecycle Management* meant — not the words but the *meaning*, the thing behind the euphemism, the operational reality that the euphemism existed to make presentable.

She did not know. She sensed — not in the data, not in the room's body language, but in the quality of her own hesitation — that the question was dangerous. Not politically dangerous. *Informationally* dangerous. That knowing the answer would change the shape of the Chair she was sitting in. That Eduardo had known the answer, and the knowing had been part of the weight she'd felt in his silences, the late nights in the office that smelled like sandalwood, the distance that had grown between them in the last years of his life — a distance she'd attributed to the weight he carried after her mother died, or to the pressure of the position, or to the simple arithmetic of a man growing old in a Chair that didn't.

She didn't ask. The slide advanced. The meeting continued.

*Not-asking is a skill the position requires.*

The small voice in the back of her mind — her father's voice, or her own, the distinction blurring — filed the thought without comment.

---

The meeting adjourned at 11:40. Standard duration. Standard outcome. The board approved the quarterly projections unanimously, ratified two infrastructure expenditure packages, and authorized the Government Relations division to proceed with the Singapore licensing renegotiation. Aurielle signed the approval documents on her datapad — biometric confirmation, the same sequence Eduardo had used, the system accepting her authority without hesitation because the system did not distinguish between the person and the position.

She walked to Eduardo's office.

Not hers. She called it Eduardo's office even in her own mind, three weeks in, because the room had not yet agreed to belong to her. The corridor from the Executive Chamber was thirty meters of the same dark wood paneling, the same recessed lighting, the same temperature-controlled silence. Her shoes — different from the gala, lower heel, authority without theater — made no sound on the carpet. She passed two security personnel who nodded without speaking. She passed the executive assistant's station — empty, the position unfilled since Eduardo's assistant had taken administrative leave the morning after the assassination and had not returned.

The office door opened to her biometrics. She stepped inside and the air changed.

Sandalwood.

Three weeks and the cologne was still there — embedded in the leather of the desk chair, the upholstery of the reading alcove, the curtains that framed the floor-to-ceiling window. NitroCore's atmospheric systems scrubbed everything above particulate level, but the cologne had seeped deeper than particulate. It was molecular. It was in the grain of the furniture the way memory was in the grain of the body — less a presence than an afterimage, the scent of a man who had occupied this room so completely that his absence was itself a kind of occupation.

She sat at the desk. The chair was not the same model as the boardroom — this one was older, heavier, a piece Eduardo had brought from the Singapore compound when he'd transferred the corporate headquarters to Neo-Shanghai in 2161. The leather was darker. It did not adjust. It held Eduardo's shape the way a mold holds the impression of what was poured into it, and when Aurielle sat in it she felt the negative space of his body around hers — broader shoulders, heavier frame, the posture of a man who had occupied chairs as if occupying territory.

She placed the water glass on her left. Opened the quarterly report on the first datapad. Started from the last page.

*Recommendations: Maintain current extraction and refinement targets. Authorize Q1 2175 infrastructure expenditure (Packages A and B). Defer Sump Division infrastructure maintenance review pending Legacy Protocol 9 reassessment.*

Legacy Protocol 9.

She hadn't encountered the term before. Not in the quarterly report, not in the transition briefings, not in the weeks of institutional orientation that Thorne had supervised with the meticulous patience of a man who understood that the position required knowledge before it required judgment. The term appeared once, in the final recommendation, embedded in a sentence that was otherwise unremarkable — a deferral, a reassessment, the bureaucratic language of a decision postponed. She would have missed it if she hadn't been reading from the last page.

She opened the second datapad. Cross-referenced. The Q4 infrastructure status report, Sump Division — the same data that had occupied slide seventeen. Containment expenditure: 40.3% above projected budget. The number was flagged with a single annotation: *LP9 applies. C-Suite only.*

LP9. Legacy Protocol 9. C-Suite only.

She opened the third datapad. The classified intelligence brief from that morning — the physical copy delivered at 06:00 and collected by a security officer at 07:30, but the Chair's secured terminal retained a read-only copy for exactly this kind of cross-referencing. She scrolled to the infrastructure section. The Sump Division summary was two paragraphs, both sanitized to the point of opacity. But at the bottom, in a font size one point smaller than the body text — small enough to be formatting, not small enough to be invisible — a reference: *For Legacy Protocol 9 context, contact Director of Operations.*

Director of Operations.

Thorne.

She placed the datapad down. Picked up the water glass. Did not drink.

The room smelled like sandalwood and the window showed the Spires catching the mid-morning light — amber and clean, the color of the grid, the color of the quarterly projections that were excellent, the color of the numbers that added up to a story in which NitroCore was prospering and the world was stable and the Chair was occupied by a woman who had inherited it by blood and was performing it with the institutional fluency her father had spent twenty years installing.

She rotated her left wrist. Slowly.

Then she messaged Thorne.

---

He arrived in fourteen minutes. She timed it — not consciously, but the small voice counted. Fourteen minutes meant he'd been in the building, probably on the executive floors. It also meant he hadn't rushed. Thorne never rushed. Rushing implied that the situation had exceeded the plan, and Thorne's plans did not get exceeded.

He entered without knocking — the door opened to his biometrics, which meant Eduardo had granted him permanent access and Aurielle hadn't revoked it, which meant the system still treated Thorne as a permanent feature of this office the way the sandalwood was a permanent feature of the air.

"You read the quarterly from the last page," he said.

Not a question. An observation. He'd predicted this — predicted which detail she'd find, predicted that she'd find it because she read from the back, predicted that she'd message him because the reference directed her to him. He'd predicted it or he'd arranged it. The distinction, with Thorne, was not always available.

"Legacy Protocol 9," she said.

He closed the door. Took the chair across from the desk — not the reading alcove, not the window seat, the formal visitor's chair. She noticed the choice. It positioned him below her sightline by six centimeters, a deference that was either habitual or deliberate. With Thorne, the answer was always deliberate.

"Your father established LP9 in 2168," Thorne said. "Three years after the São Paulo incident. Seven years after the 2161 VEC containment assessment flagged the first throughput-breach correlations. It classifies all data relating to Sump infrastructure sustainability — long-term viability models, containment cost projections, RCI trend analysis for metropolitan zones — under executive access only. C-Suite. No divisional heads, no board liaisons, no external auditors."

His voice was the same voice from the corridor. Level. Sequential. Each sentence a brick.

"The memo language is specific." He produced a datapad — his own, already queued. "'Classified under Legacy Protocol 9. Distribution beyond executive chain constitutes breach of corporate sovereignty.' Your father signed it. I countersigned."

She took the datapad. Read the memo. It was short — half a page, institutional language, the kind of document that existed to create a boundary and then enforce it through the weight of its own classification. She read it twice.

"Why?"

Thorne folded his hands. The same posture as the boardroom. The same composure. She could not read him — she could read most people in a room, could parse micro-expressions and vocal patterns with the fluency Eduardo had trained into her, but Thorne's surface was uniform. Not blank. *Managed.* Every visible element calibrated to communicate precisely what he chose to communicate and nothing more.

"Because the real numbers require context," he said. "And context, at this level, is a responsibility. Not a right."

He paused. Selecting.

"RCI is climbing in three metropolitan zones. Neo-Shanghai, São Paulo, Mumbai. Neo-Shanghai is worst. The trend has been consistent for eighteen months — not spiking, not stabilizing. Climbing. Slowly. The kind of slow that looks like noise until you overlay it with the containment expenditure data, and then it looks like a line that doesn't flatten."

She waited. Her hands were flat on the desk.

"Containment is forty percent over budget because containment is growing. More 'shimmers.' More RCI fluctuations in the Deep Sump sectors. More monitoring hours, more Stalker deployments, more infrastructure reinforcement. The Sump Division's 'lifecycle management' is the budget line that absorbs these costs — manages the infrastructure that sits between the Confluence and the population above it. When containment expenditure goes up, lifecycle management absorbs the increase. When lifecycle management absorbs the increase, the infrastructure maintenance it was supposed to fund gets deferred."

"Deferred to where?"

"To the next quarter. And the quarter after that. The maintenance backlog is currently fourteen months. Junction integrity across Sectors 4 through 9 is averaging sixty-seven percent. Your father's threshold was seventy. Below seventy, the conduits become — " He paused again. Selection. " — less predictable."

Less predictable. She heard the word he'd chosen and the word he hadn't. Not *dangerous.* Not *failing.* *Less predictable.* A word that preserved the institution's language while gesturing toward a reality the language was designed to contain.

"The correlation between throughput density and breach frequency is classified above LP9 — that's VEC jurisdiction, Annex B, the kind of data that moves through channels neither of us nominally controls. But the *effects* of the correlation are in your budget. You're paying for containment that's growing because the thing being contained is growing, and the growth rate has not responded to any intervention your father authorized in eleven years."

He let the sentence settle.

"Your father managed this. The budget, the deferrals, the classification. He managed the information architecture that keeps these numbers inside LP9 and outside the board's quarterly review. He managed the relationship with the VEC that keeps the Annex B data separate from the LP9 data so that no single document contains both the cause and the cost. He managed it for eleven years."

"Now you do."

The words landed the way Thorne's words always landed — not as pressure but as architecture. The sentence didn't push. It *placed.* It set down a fact the way you set down a stone in a wall, precisely, load-bearing, in the position where the structure required it.

Aurielle's hands were still flat on the desk. She noticed this. Noticed that she had not reached for her wrist, had not shifted in the chair, had not broken the posture that the Chair required. The composure was holding. The training was holding. Eduardo's lessons were holding — the voice, the stillness, the institutional surface that projected control regardless of what was moving underneath.

Underneath, the small voice was doing arithmetic.

Forty percent over budget. Eighteen months of climbing RCI. Fourteen-month maintenance backlog. Junction integrity at sixty-seven percent against a seventy-percent threshold. Three metropolitan zones. Neo-Shanghai worst.

She processed the numbers the way she processed everything — systemically, seeking the cascade, the second-order consequence, the downstream implication that the first-order data obscured. If containment costs continued to climb at the current rate and maintenance continued to defer, then junction integrity would continue to decline. If junction integrity declined below — whatever the threshold was, whatever number lived in the VEC's Annex B data that she didn't have access to yet — then the infrastructure between the Deep Sump and the population above it would become not *less predictable* but something else. Something the system was spending forty percent over budget to prevent.

"What happens," she said, "if the containment expenditure stops being sufficient?"

Thorne looked at her. The first direct eye contact since he'd sat down. His expression had not changed — the same managed surface, the same calibrated neutrality — but the aperture behind his eyes contracted — the same surface, tighter focus. As if, of all the questions she could have asked, this was the one he'd been waiting for.

"That," he said, "is why Legacy Protocol 9 exists."

He stood. Collected his datapad. The conversation was over — not because the question had been answered but because the question had been *placed*, deposited in the same architecture that held the numbers and the classification and the eleven years of Eduardo's management. The answer would come. Not today. Not in this conversation. It would come in briefings and budget reviews and classified documents and quiet conversations in this office that smelled like sandalwood, delivered piece by piece, brick by brick, the way Thorne built everything — patiently, precisely, letting her intelligence do the work.

"You asked the right question," he said from the doorway. Not praise. Assessment. "Eduardo asked the wrong one. He asked how to fix it."

The door closed behind him.

---

Aurielle sat in Eduardo's chair for twenty-three minutes after Thorne left.

She did not open the datapads. She did not review the quarterly. She did not message Chen-Nakamura or draft a memo or begin the institutional processes that the morning's board meeting required — the follow-up communications, the divisional directives, the cascade of institutional actions that flowed from the Chair like water from a source.

She sat in the office that smelled like her dead father's cologne and looked at the desk he'd sat behind for eleven years while managing the numbers Thorne had just given her. The walnut surface was clean. The water glass caught the ambient light and held it — amber, the color of the grid. The window behind her showed the Spires in mid-morning, towers rising into a sky that was clear and blue and visible from this altitude in a way it was not visible from below.

She thought about slide seventeen. *Sump Infrastructure Lifecycle Management.* The twelve seconds it had been on screen. The fifteen faces that hadn't reacted. The question she hadn't asked — not because she couldn't, not because the room had silenced her, but because some part of her had known, before Thorne explained anything, that the answer lived behind a door she was not ready to open.

The door had opened anyway. Thorne had opened it. Not pushed her through — he never pushed. He'd opened the door and shown her the corridor and told her that her father had walked it for eleven years and that the corridor was now hers, and the walking was the job, and the job was the Chair.

*Your father managed this. Now you do.*

Not a threat. Not a command. A *coronation.*

Her left wrist had started rotating — slow, unconscious, the phantom fracture answering the way it always answered when the world delivered information her body processed before her mind caught up. She noticed it. She stopped it. She placed both hands flat on the desk — Eduardo's desk, the Spanish walnut, the surface that held nothing because empty surfaces projected control — and she held them there until the stillness was not performance but fact.

The handkerchief was in the top drawer. She knew it was there. Cleaned, folded, white silk with bloodstains that the cleaning had not fully removed. She did not open the drawer.

The small voice in the back of her mind — the one that calculated, that optimized, that she was beginning to suspect had always been there, waiting for the right numbers to calculate with — was quiet. Still running. *Processing.* Running the arithmetic she couldn't yet see the edges of, working the variables Thorne had placed in front of her the way you place pieces on a board before the game begins. RCI climbing. Containment growing. Maintenance deferred. Integrity declining.

And beneath all of it, a question she hadn't asked Thorne because she'd sensed — the way she'd sensed the danger of slide seventeen, the way she'd sensed the sealed quality of Thorne's suit at the gala — that the answer was not something you received. It was something you *became.*

*What happens when the containment isn't sufficient?*

She knew what happened. Not the specifics — those would come, in briefings and budgets and the slow institutional education Thorne was conducting with the patience of a man who had been teaching this curriculum for longer than she'd been alive. But the shape of it. The architecture. The thing the numbers were describing, the thing Legacy Protocol 9 existed to classify, the thing her father had managed for eleven years and had never told her about — not because he didn't trust her, but because telling her would have meant naming it, and naming it would have meant acknowledging that the institution she'd inherited was not a machine that occasionally produced unfortunate outcomes but a machine that was *designed* to produce them. That the outcomes were not bugs. They were the product. The budget line that absorbed the cost of breach containment was the same budget line that deferred the infrastructure maintenance that might have prevented the breaches, and the deferral was not negligence but *policy*, and the policy was classified because classification was how the institution maintained the distance between what it did and what it said it did.

The architecture of looking elsewhere.

She stood. Straightened the datapads. Positioned the water glass precisely where it had been. Checked the room — everything in its place, the desk clear, the chair pushed in, the office restored to the condition Eduardo would have expected. The sandalwood settled around her like weather.

She did not look out the window. She knew what she would see. The Spires. The sky. The city stretching downward into a density she had never visited, a stratum she had never walked, a world she was now responsible for managing — *lifecycle management*, the quarterly said, as if lives were infrastructure and infrastructure had lifecycles and the cycles could be *managed* by someone sitting in a chair at the top of a tower that hummed so faintly she'd been trained to hear it as silence.

She walked to the door. Paused. Turned back.

The drawer. Top left.

She didn't open it. She didn't need to. She knew what was inside — the handkerchief, white silk, folded, the bloodstain that wouldn't fully clean because some stains were structural rather than superficial. Thorne's handkerchief. The first thing he'd given her. The thing she kept because keeping it was easier than understanding why she'd been given it, and understanding why she'd been given it would require her to stand in the same room as the question she'd sealed in the partition three weeks ago and still could not look at directly.

*He knew.*

She left the office. The door closed behind her. The sandalwood remained.

# Chapter 8

## White Noise

> *"We do not ask you to rebel. We ask you to describe what you see."*
>
> — *The Kindling Letters*, Vol. II

---nn## Draft v1

Nuwa was cooking when he came through the door.

He smelled it before he saw her — soy paste and chili oil and the sharp mineral note of reconstituted protein heating in a pan that was older than both of them. The smell cut through the corridor's chemical sweetness like a blade. Real food. Not the subsidized ration packs that came vacuum-sealed with the Provision logo and a calorie count that assumed you spent your shift sitting down. Nuwa had found something at the market — actual vegetables, or close enough. She did this sometimes. Came home from the textile plant and went straight to the Hum Market with the credits she'd set aside from the household fund, the ones Fuxi pretended not to notice were missing because the argument about it was more expensive than the food.

She was standing at the heating element with her back to him. Her hair was shorter than last month — she'd cut it herself, the way she always did, with the shears from the plant. The cut was uneven at the back. She didn't care. Nuwa's relationship with her appearance was purely functional — anything that could get caught in machinery got cut, and everything else was irrelevant. She was wearing the grey coverall from the plant, sleeves pushed to her elbows. Her forearms were stained. The textile recycling process used a chemical solvent that turned skin a faint violet where it made contact, and Nuwa's hands and wrists were mapped with it — a topography of eight-hour shifts and inadequate protective equipment and a plant manager who had filed the requisition for new gloves six months ago and received, in response, a revised safety protocol that reclassified the solvent exposure threshold.

"Boots," she said, without turning around.

Fuxi looked down at his boots. Orange dust. Deep Sump residue. The mat by the door was right there.

"I'm inside."

"You're on my floor."

He stepped onto the mat. Pulled his boots off. The apartment floor was cold through his socks — the concrete transmitted the temperature the way it transmitted the hum, evenly, without preference, a medium through which everything traveled. He set the boots on the mat, side by side, the way Nuwa had been asking him to do for three years and the way he'd been doing for approximately one.

She turned around. Her face was the same shape as his — their mother's jaw, their father's forehead, the Lin geometry that marked them as siblings before they opened their mouths. But where Fuxi's face had been compressed by the Deep Sump into an expression that defaulted to neutral, Nuwa's face was in constant negotiation with itself. She was twenty-four and she looked twenty-four and she looked older than twenty-four and she looked like someone who had decided that looking tired was a waste of energy she could spend on something else.

"You look terrible," she said.

"Standard."

"Worse than standard. Sit."

He sat. The table was a slab of composite bolted to the wall — everything in the apartment was bolted to something, a habit of construction from when the Sump residential blocks had been built over active conduit lines and the vibration had been strong enough to move furniture. The vibration was weaker now, at this depth. Barely perceptible through the table's surface. Fuxi rested his hands flat on it anyway and felt the hum — faint, constant, the building's pulse carried through concrete and steel and composite and into the bones of his wrists. Home frequency. Different from the Deep Sump's bass drone. Thinner. Quicker. A domestic hum.

Nuwa set a bowl in front of him. Reconstituted protein with chili oil, soy paste, and something green that might have been bok choy or might have been a convincing imitation. Steam rose from the surface and the smell was close and real and human in a way that the monitoring bay never was.

"Eat," she said. "Before it gets cold and becomes evidence."

"Evidence of what?"

"Of the fact that I spent twenty creds on vegetables instead of putting it toward the frame fund. Eat fast. Destroy the evidence."

He ate. The food was good. Better than good — it was specific. It tasted like something someone had chosen to make, not something extruded from a processing line and sealed in a packet with a barcode. Nuwa's cooking was like her conversation: layered, deliberate, assembled from whatever was available into something that exceeded the sum of its components. She sat across from him with her own bowl and ate the way she always ate — quickly, efficiently, one hand holding the bowl close, the other working the chopsticks with a precision that came from the same muscle memory she used at the plant, sorting textiles by weight and grade, her hands reading material the way Fuxi's hands read pipe casings.

The hum was in the walls. In the floor. In the table between them. It was the sound of the conduit network running through the building's infrastructure — the smaller distribution lines that branched off the trunk system and fed the Sump residential blocks with the nitro that powered the lights, the heating elements, the frame relay stations, the water recyclers. Everything. The hum was the sound of everything working. It was their white noise. They had grown up inside it, slept inside it, eaten ten thousand meals inside it. Fuxi did not hear it the way he did not hear his own breathing — it was present and constant and below the threshold of attention, and the only time he noticed it was when it changed.

It had not changed.

"So," Nuwa said. She set her bowl down and leaned back and looked at him with the expression that meant she was about to build a case. "The P-3."

"The P-3."

"Stall 14 guy says one more week on the hold. After that it goes back on the table."

"We're two months into the savings plan."

"Two months into *your* savings plan. I have a different plan."

Fuxi set down his chopsticks. "What plan."

"Yuen's plant is doing a round of transfers. Mid-Level textile operations. Quality-control positions. They need people with experience on the sorting line who can interface with the QC monitoring system, which requires" — she held up one finger — "a functional frame with AR overlay that doesn't render my supervisor as a floating torso."

"The P-3."

"The P-3. With the sensory filter. Which also means I stop getting the headaches at work, which means I stop burning two credits a week on the suppressants, which means the math actually works if you run it forward six months instead of looking at it as a lump expense."

Fuxi picked up his chopsticks again. The food was getting cold. He ate and listened to her build the case, brick by brick, the same way she'd built it over frame messages in the Deep Sump — but hearing it in her voice, in person, with her hands moving as she talked, was different. She used her hands the way he used monitoring data. Each gesture was a data point. The finger counting savings. The flat palm pressing down on the table as she laid out the transfer requirements. The quick sweep through her hair — the uneven cut, the shears she wasn't supposed to have — when she hit the part about transit permits.

"Transit permits are locked for the quarter," Fuxi said.

"Transit permits are locked for Sump-to-Spires. Sump-to-Mid-Level transfers on employer sponsorship are processed separately. Yuen's plant has a standing arrangement with GridLine for employee mobility within the industrial classification. It's a different queue."

"You've already checked."

"I've already checked."

He looked at her. She looked back. The conduit glow came through the frosted polymer window and cast its orange light across the table, across her face, across the violet staining on her hands. In the Deep Sump, the orange was absolute — it saturated everything, turned the world monochrome. Up here, in the apartment, it was diluted by the overhead fixture that Nuwa had repaired herself three weeks ago when the building maintenance had failed to respond to the fourth request. The light in the apartment was orange and white and something between the two. It turned Nuwa's face into a study in warmth that was not entirely the conduit's doing.

"Mid-Level," he said.

"Mid-Level."

"That's up."

"That's the point, Fuxi."

He ate another bite. Chewed. The protein had gone cold and the texture had changed — the reconstitution process was heat-dependent, and cooled reconstituted protein had a grain to it that reminded him of gasket material. He ate it anyway.

"The seniority I have with the service—"

"—keeps you in the Deep Sump maintaining trunk-lines for ten hours a day while the RCI readings climb and the suppressants your coworkers take make their hands slow and the overtime they offer for the Resonance District section comes at double rate because everyone who works there for more than six months files medical claims that the company settles out of the emergency discretionary budget that technically doesn't exist." She said all of this without raising her voice. The words came fast and flat and organized, the way sorted textiles came off her line — graded by weight, by urgency, by the order in which they needed to land. "Your seniority is a leash, and the leash is attached to a pipe, and the pipe is getting warmer."

"The pipe is fine."

"The pipe is always fine. Until it isn't."

The hum filled the silence between them. It was a good silence — not empty, not hostile. A silence that held the shape of an argument they'd had before and would have again, an argument whose contours they both knew the way Fuxi knew the trunk-line's resonance. Familiar. Navigable. Survivable.

Nuwa picked up her bowl again. Ate. Her jaw worked with the same efficient rhythm as her hands at the sorting line. Then:

"I'm not asking you to leave. I'm asking you to let me try."

"I'm not stopping you."

"You're calculating. I can see it. You're running the math on what happens if I get the transfer and you're still down there, and the math says the rent goes up because the subsidy is tied to your service address and my contribution drops during the transition period and the net is negative for four months."

The math did say that. He had been running it since she first mentioned Yuen's transfers three days ago, the numbers cycling in the back of his mind the way monitoring data cycled across his screens — automatically, continuously, a background process that never stopped.

"Four months is manageable," he said.

"Four months is manageable." She put her bowl down. "Wait. Is that a yes?"

"That's a the-math-is-manageable."

"Coming from you that's practically a parade."

She smiled. Not large — Nuwa's smiles were compressed, the way everything in the Sump was compressed, occupying the minimum necessary space. But present. It changed the geometry of her face in a way that reminded him of their mother, and the reminder was a blade that he turned aside the way he turned aside all the blades that came at him in the space between work and sleep — not by force but by redirection, by sending the thought down a channel where it could run without cutting.

He gathered the bowls. Took them to the basin. The water came out warm — heated by the conduit lines that ran behind the wall, one of the few advantages of living inside the infrastructure. He washed the bowls and felt the hum through the water and through the basin and through his hands, which were still calibrated to the Deep Sump's frequency and which registered the apartment's hum as a high, thin cousin of the sound that lived in his bones for ten hours every shift.

"The market was busy today," Nuwa said behind him.

"Mmhm."

"I went past stall 14. The P-3 is still there. The guy remembers me."

"He remembers your creds."

"Same thing, down here." A pause. The kind of pause that had texture. "The route back was crowded. Everyone going the same way, toward the residential blocks. Normal crowd."

He heard the pause. Heard what she wasn't saying underneath it. The route from the Hum Market to their block ran past two conduit access points — heavy steel doors set into the corridor walls, marked with the NitroCore logo and the universal hazard symbol that everyone in the Sump had learned to ignore the way they'd learned to ignore the hum. The access points were where the shimmers appeared. Not often. Not predictably. But the municipal advisory had been updated twice in the last quarter — *Ambient hum levels within certified tolerance. If you experience headaches, contact NitroCore health station.* — and the advisory only updated when the readings moved.

"Normal crowd," he said.

"Normal crowd."

He set the clean bowl in the rack. Turned off the water. The basin's vibration ceased but the hum continued — walls, floor, ceiling, the constant architecture of sound that was the Sump's version of quiet.

He did not ask her what she'd seen near the conduit access point on the route back from stall 14. She did not offer. The not-asking and the not-offering were the same shape — a mutual agreement, enacted without negotiation, to keep certain observations inside the body where they could not become problems. Fuxi knew this shape. He practiced it professionally. Every shift at station 3, watching monitors 4 through 6, logging what the instruments showed and not logging what his body felt. The domestic version was gentler. Smaller. Built from love rather than protocol.

But it was the same architecture.

---

Nuwa went to bed at 22:00. She had the early shift tomorrow — textiles ran 06:00 to 14:00 on this rotation, and Nuwa's rotation started at the sorting line and ended at chemical processing, which meant she needed her hands steady and her headache manageable and her frame functional enough to read the material grade codes that the QC system projected in AR across each batch. The current frame — salvaged, second-hand, its overlay glitching near conduit junctions — was costing her accuracy. Accuracy was costing her the transfer.

The P-3 was not a luxury. It was infrastructure. Fuxi understood this the way he understood gasket tolerances — not as an abstraction but as a physical fact with physical consequences. The frame was the difference between Nuwa staying at the Sump plant and Nuwa moving to Mid-Level. Mid-Level was not the Spires. It was not escape. It was forty meters higher and marginally less orange and the hum was quieter and the transit permits were easier and the medical coverage included the solvent-exposure treatment that the Sump plant classified as elective.

Forty meters. In a city that measured status by altitude, forty meters was a life.

He sat on the bed in the dark. The blue textile was beneath him — the deep blue fabric with the interlocking circles that Nuwa had salvaged from the recycling plant because it was the bluest thing the plant had ever processed and because everything in the Sump was orange and because she wanted one thing that wasn't. He ran his hand across it. The texture was smooth, worn soft by use, and in the dark it was just a fabric, but in the conduit glow it was the only thing in the apartment that wasn't the color of nitro.

His hand found the multitool in his jacket pocket. His father's. Jun Lin's. Stainless steel, heavy for its size, the handle worn to a polish by decades of use — first in his father's hands, maintaining the same trunk-lines that Fuxi maintained now, and then in Fuxi's, carried every shift but rarely used for its intended purpose. The service-issue toolkit was better. Newer. Calibrated. The multitool was obsolete. He carried it anyway. The weight of it in his pocket was a specific thing — not comfort, not memory, not sentiment. *Presence.* His father's hands had held this tool in the same corridors where Fuxi's hands worked now, and his father had died of the cumulative exposure that the company medical officer called "chronic resonance fatigue syndrome" and that the Deep Sump crews called "the hum got him," and the multitool was what remained.

He turned it in his fingers. The hum came through the walls and the floor and the building's bones and settled behind his eyes the way it always did — a pressure that was not quite a headache and not quite nothing. Occupational tinnitus. Certified tolerance.

Monitor 6 had read 27.1 at the end of his shift today. Baseline. Normal. The spike from three weeks ago — 31.2, hold, linear decay — had not recurred. The junction housing 4E-9 inspection he'd recommended had been scheduled, conducted, and closed with a finding of "no anomaly detected." The system had self-corrected. The log had cycled through the active queue and was aging toward the ninety-day archive. In fourteen more shifts, it would be gone.

But the shape.

He kept coming back to the shape. The linear decline. The clean, precise descent from peak to baseline as if the reading had known where it was going and had gone there deliberately. Not a system decaying. Not a fluctuation self-correcting through the accumulated friction of redundancy margins and flow regulators. A line. Drawn from here to there. Straight.

He had not told Nuwa about the spike. He had not told Nuwa about the shape. This was not deception — Nuwa did not ask about his readings the way he did not ask about her solvent exposure, and the mutual not-asking was how they lived inside a system that generated information faster than it generated the capacity to act on it. You learned what to hold and what to set down. You learned which data points were actionable and which were the ambient noise of living inside infrastructure that was a hundred and twenty years old and running at three times its design specification. Most of the noise was just noise. The hum was just the hum. The readings self-corrected.

Fuxi sat on the blue textile in the dark apartment in the Sump of Neo-Shanghai and held his father's multitool and listened to the hum that had been his white noise since the day he was born and did not think about the shape of the decline on monitor 6 and did not think about what Nuwa had not said about the route back from stall 14 and did not think about the municipal advisory that had been updated twice in the last quarter for a hum that was within certified tolerance.

He thought about the P-3. One more month for the creds. Four more after that — the transition, the net-negative, the rent subsidy gap. The math was manageable. Nuwa would get the frame. Nuwa would get the transfer. Nuwa would move up — forty meters, a different plant, better medical, a frame that worked. He would stay in the Deep Sump because the Deep Sump was where the work was and the work was what kept them fed and housed and saving. This was the arrangement. This was the architecture of their lives — Fuxi below, maintaining the system that maintained the city, and Nuwa above, or soon above, rising through the narrow pathways that existed for people who were precise and fast and willing to cut their own hair with stolen shears.

He would stay. She would rise. He would keep the pipes running and the hum constant and the monitors green and his hands steady and his reports filed and his questions unasked, because the questions were not actionable and the answers were not survivable and the system self-corrected and his sister needed five more months — one for the frame, four for the climb.

Outside, the conduit glow pulsed through the frosted polymer window. Orange. Constant. The color of the world that worked. The hum carried through the building and into the bones of a man sitting in the dark with a dead man's tool in his hands, and the system was running, and the system was fine, and the readings were within tolerance, and the advisory had been updated only twice, and somewhere two hundred meters below, the trunk-lines carried what they carried at volumes that were classified and temperatures that were rising and in a pattern that — if you looked at it from exactly the right angle, and if you had spent six years learning what the instruments couldn't show you — was not quite noise.

# Chapter 9

## Dead Drop

> *"The difference between a rumor and a report is one surviving source."*
>
> — *The Wire: Collected Dispatches*, Mirelle Dubois

---nn## Draft v1

The room cost four hundred credits a week and smelled like the last occupant's cooking oil. Mirelle Dubois sat cross-legged on the floor with the contents of her investigation laid out in front of her in three rows.

Row one: paper. Actual paper — not printed from a frame, not generated from a template, but written by hand on thirty-two sheets of recycled pulp she'd bought from a vendor in the Hum Market who sold it by weight and didn't ask what it was for. Handwritten notes. Handwritten timelines. Handwritten names. Dao Suen. Chen Yue. Fourteen others — fourteen names she'd confirmed across five sectors in the last eight weeks, fourteen conduit maintenance workers who had walked toward trunk-line access points and not walked back, fourteen Feed entries that said *relocated* or *reassigned* or *credential transferred* in the same bureaucratic register that made disappearance sound like paperwork.

She'd written the names in chronological order. The first one she could date was eleven months before Dao — a converter station tech in Sector 7, name of Bai Lin, whose daughter had filed a missing persons report that was reclassified as an employment dispute within forty-eight hours. The most recent was nine days ago — a conduit welder in Sector 2, name of Ramos, whose partner had posted on the underground mesh and had the post removed within six hours for *unverified personnel claims.*

Sixteen disappearances. Five sectors. All within two hundred meters of a trunk-line junction or access point. All reclassified by the Feed within days. All invisible to anyone who wasn't cross-referencing municipal employment records with NitroCore infrastructure maps with residential block demographic data — and nobody was cross-referencing those things because nobody had access to all three databases simultaneously except Mirelle, who had access to none of them legitimately and all of them through the particular combination of borrowed credentials, cultivated sources, and patient, methodical theft that she called reporting.

Row two: data. Two encrypted drives — thumb-sized, solid-state, commercial hardware she'd bought in the Hum Market and wiped to factory spec before loading. Drive one held the compiled dataset: sixteen disappearances, RCI readings from eleven of the sixteen sites, NitroCore's public infrastructure reports for the last three years showing a pattern of tolerance-band widening that tracked with the disappearance timeline, and the Feed notices — every *relocated,* every *reassigned,* every *no disruption expected,* cataloged by date, sector, and proximity to conduit infrastructure.

Drive two was a mirror. Identical data. Different encryption key. One would stay with her. One would not.

Row three: her notes. Not the investigation — the *analysis.* What she thought the data meant. What she couldn't prove. What she suspected. Written in the raw, angry register she never published — the voice that existed between the clean sentences of her filed pieces and the careful inventory of her evidence. *They're not relocating people. They're losing them. The infrastructure is eating its workers and the company is filing the losses as transfers and nobody is counting because the count belongs to NitroCore and NitroCore has decided that sixteen is within tolerance.*

She didn't know if that was true. She didn't know what *the infrastructure is eating its workers* meant in mechanical terms. She had no mechanism. She had geography and timing and a Feed that lied and families who knew it lied and a chalk tradition on concrete walls that documented the truth in the only medium nobody could reclassify.

She sat with the three rows in front of her and turned her stylus end over end between her fingers. The stylus was a holdover — she wrote on paper because paper didn't ping the mesh and didn't get swept in a frame audit and didn't exist on any server NitroCore could subpoena. Same model she'd used at the bureau in Abidjan, where she'd learned that the difference between a journalist and a target was how many copies of the story existed and who held them.

One copy was not enough. One copy meant that removing her removed the story.

She picked up the second drive and held it in her palm. Small. Smooth. Cold from the floor.

She put the drive in her jacket pocket. She packed the paper into the false lining of her coat — thirty-two sheets, flat, invisible to a pat-down, felt like just another part of her frame, but findable if you knew where to squeeze. She put the first drive in her boot, under the insole, next to the RCI sensor she still hadn't returned.

She left the room. The door locked behind her — mechanical, no mesh connection, the reason she'd chosen this particular room in this particular building in Sump Sector 3, six blocks from the brightline and three strata above and below anything NitroCore would call interesting.

---

The route to the Resonance District was not direct. Mirelle had planned three variations, each calibrated to the shift schedule of the transit corridors and the patrol patterns she'd mapped over five weeks of walking the same routes at irregular intervals.

Today: Variation B. South through the Sector 3 commercial strip — crowded at this hour, the second-shift workers flowing toward the transit stairs in a current dense enough to disappear into. East at the Sector 4 junction, where the commercial corridor narrowed and the surveillance coverage thinned because NitroCore had downgraded their junction-access cameras to motion-detect after the last infrastructure budget reallocation. South again through the trunk-line underpass, where the hum was louder and the crowd was thinner and the light shifted from standard Sump-orange to something deeper — the saturated amber of first-generation conduit infrastructure, pipes laid a century and a half ago, the metal walls worn translucent by decades of nitro throughput.

She adjusted her ocular implant. Left eye — a subtle iris shift as the gain compensated for the darker spectrum. The implant was seven years old, mid-range, the kind of hardware a Sump worker might have. She'd had it tuned by an augmentation tech in the Hum Market — different contact from the Chén Academy engineer who'd calibrated her RCI sensor, different skill set, same principle: pay in favors, never in traceable credit. It recorded what she saw without pinging any network. The data lived in local storage behind her left orbit and transferred to her burner drive via physical cable once a day, in private, with the frame powered down.

The Resonance District announced itself before she reached it. Not visually — the streets looked the same, the same narrow corridors, the same low ceilings, the same feed-screens scrolling the same indifferent updates. It announced itself in her bones. The hum changed. Deepened. The vibration that had been a background presence since she'd left the commercial strip became a physical pressure — in her jaw, her sternum, the bone behind her ears. The Resonance District sat on first-generation trunk-lines, six of them converging beneath the neighborhood at the highest-throughput junction in the city, and the sound they produced was not the manageable drone of the regular Sump. It was older. Louder. The kind of sound that lived in your skeleton and rearranged your sleep.

She'd been in the Sump almost seven months. The nitro-ear had started three weeks ago — a faint, high-pitched tone in her right ear that surfaced when the ambient hum dropped, like a ringing that had always been there but needed quiet to be heard. It wasn't quiet, of course. There was no quiet in the Sump. But there were gradations, and her ear had started finding them.

The district's streets were narrower than the commercial strip. Fewer feed-screens. More counter-surveillance hardware in storefront windows — mesh scramblers, frame jammers, signal-dampening paint. The Hum Market was two blocks east, and its economy bled into the surrounding blocks: information brokerage, black-market ampoules, identity credential leasing, all conducted in the chronic high-RCI environment that kept corporate security from staying longer than they had to. The Resonance District policed itself by discomfort, not law. If the hum didn't drive you out, the Hollow Legion's territorial markers would, and if those didn't, the readings above thirty would make the decision for you the next time your frame flagged a health advisory.

Mirelle's frame didn't flag health advisories. She'd disabled that function in her second week.

She checked her route. No tails — she'd verified at three checkpoints built into the variation: a reflective surface at the Sector 4 junction, a deliberate stop at a food vendor where she could watch the approach corridor while buying something she wouldn't eat, and a left turn at the trunk-line underpass that committed her to a thirty-meter stretch with one exit and clear rear sightlines. Clean. Or clean enough. Certainty was a luxury she'd stopped expecting around the time the third source declined to speak to her.

She turned onto the street where Talia Ravid kept her node.

---

The node didn't look like anything. That was the point. From the street it was a repair shop — frame servicing, implant calibration, the kind of business that existed in every Sump commercial strip and attracted exactly the right kind of foot traffic: transient, anonymous, people who needed hardware fixed and didn't want to explain where the hardware came from.

The front room had a counter, a woman Mirelle had never seen before, and a display of refurbished frame components arranged on a backlit shelf. The woman looked up. Mirelle gave the current month's phrase — six words in Cantonese that changed every thirty days and which Talia distributed through a dead-letter system that required physical presence to retrieve.

The woman pressed something under the counter. A door behind the display shelf slid open with the mechanical efficiency of hardware that got used several times a day.

Mirelle walked through.

The back room was larger than the front — the building's exterior footprint lying about its interior, a common Resonance District arrangement, walls shifted, spaces repurposed, the architecture as fluid as the information that moved through it. The room was cool, well-lit by a spectrum that wasn't conduit-orange, and dense with hardware: storage racks, encrypted relay stations, three displays running data streams Mirelle didn't try to read, not because she didn't want to — because she *did* want to — but she was only four minutes early to a meeting she should've been five minutes early to. The hum was present but muted — Talia had invested in insulation, the serious kind, the kind that cost more than the hardware it protected.

Talia Ravid sat at a workstation in the center of the room with her back to the door. She didn't turn around.

"You're four minutes early," she said. Her voice was even, unhurried — the register of someone who tracked time the way other people tracked weather. Automatically. Without investment. "I charge for wasted time. I don't charge for early."

"I appreciate the distinction."

Talia turned. Ghanaian-Israeli, ageless in the way that good augmentation made possible — her skin smooth, her hair close-cropped, her eyes carrying the faint luminescent ring of military-grade optical hardware several generations above what Mirelle had in her left orbit. She wore a plain gray coverall. No jewelry. The only thing on her workstation besides the displays was a mug of tea and a data interface that looked like it could process more information per second than The Wire's entire Paris bureau.

"The package," Talia said. Not a question.

Mirelle reached into her jacket and set the second drive on the workstation. Small. Smooth. The whole weight of sixteen names in a piece of hardware lighter than a coin.

Talia didn't touch it. She looked at it the way an appraiser examines an uncut stone — evaluating not the object but the market it would move through.

"Contents."

"Sixteen confirmed disappearances across five Sump sectors. All conduit maintenance workers. All within two hundred meters of trunk-line infrastructure. All reclassified by the Feed as relocated or reassigned. RCI readings from eleven of the sixteen sites — all above baseline. NitroCore infrastructure reports showing tolerance-band widening that tracks with the disappearance timeline. Feed notices, demographic data, source interviews anonymized. My analysis."

"*Your* analysis." Talia's eyebrow shifted — a millimeter, the smallest possible expression of professional interest. "You're editorializing."

"I'm *contextualizing.* The data speaks for itself. The analysis is what the data says if you listen."

"My clients prefer to do their own listening."

"Your clients can delete the analysis file. It's partitioned."

Talia's mouth moved in what might have been approval. She picked up the drive and inserted it into the interface. Data structures populated on the displays, file trees expanding, the encrypted contents unpacking into Talia's system with the smooth efficiency of hardware designed for exactly this kind of intake.

"Clean encryption," Talia said. "Your contact at the Academy?"

Mirelle didn't answer. Talia didn't expect her to.

The data finished loading. Talia scrolled through the file tree — fast, practiced, her eyes moving with the faint luminescent pulse of her optical hardware processing the information faster than her conscious attention could follow. She paused on the RCI readings. Paused again on the geographic overlay — the map of disappearances laid against the conduit infrastructure map, sixteen points across five sectors, all clustering around trunk-line junctions.

"That's a pattern," Talia said.

"That's the story."

"It's a pattern. It becomes a story when someone publishes it. Right now it's a dataset with a compelling geographic correlation that any competent analyst could attribute to proximity bias." She turned from the display. "Why are you bringing this to me instead of your editor?"

"My editor wants a second source. A body. A VEC report. Something that isn't chalk on a wall."

"Your editor is correct."

"My editor is in Paris. Eight time zones from the nearest chalk name."

Talia regarded her. The luminescent ring in her eyes pulsed — slow, processing. Then she reached for her tea and took a sip. The mug was chipped. The tea smelled like mint.

"What do you want?"

"Dead-hand registration."

The room's ambient hum shifted register — or Mirelle imagined it did. The attenuated vibration through Talia's insulated walls. The quiet tick of cooling systems. The electrical whisper of hardware doing what hardware did.

"Terms," Talia said. Her voice hadn't changed. The word was procedural. She might have been discussing a parts order.

"Seventy-two-hour rolling window. I ping a designated address every seventy-two hours. If I miss two consecutive windows —"

"One hundred forty-four hours."

"— the package auto-distributes to a pre-set recipient list."

"How many recipients?"

"Three."

"I'll need the addresses encrypted and sealed. I don't see them. I don't know them. The auto-distribute triggers on missed windows and routes to addresses I can't read. That's the architecture."

"That's the architecture."

Talia set down her tea. "The Babel price."

Black Babel didn't work for free, and Talia didn't work for money — or not only for money. The node's economy ran on information, and information was what Mirelle had.

"Source network metadata," Mirelle said. "Anonymized. No names, no locations, no identifying details. The structure — how many sources, what sectors, what access tiers, what institutional affiliations. The pattern of my network without the identities."

"That's valuable."

"That's the point."

"It's valuable because it tells my other clients where to look for the kind of people who talk to journalists. You understand that."

Mirelle understood it. The metadata wouldn't identify her sources — she'd stripped every node to its categorical skeleton. But the skeleton was valuable. It told anyone who bought it that someone had cultivated sources at these institutional levels, in these sectors, with these access patterns. A map of vulnerability — not of the sources themselves but of the gaps in NitroCore's information security that the sources represented.

"I understand it."

"And you're comfortable with it."

"I'm comfortable with the tradeoff."

Talia studied her. The luminescent ring was steady — not processing, *observing.* "Most of my clients negotiate. They want a better price. They want to pay less. You're paying exactly what I quoted and you're not pushing back." She paused. "That tells me something about your timeline. You're not in a hurry because the story is ready. You're in a hurry because you're not sure you'll be around when it is."

Mirelle picked up her stylus from the workstation where she'd set it down and turned it end over end between her fingers. Once. Twice.

"Register the dead-hand," she said.

Talia held her gaze for another second. Then she turned back to the interface and her fingers moved — fast, precise, the mechanical vocabulary of someone who had built and maintained information architecture for longer than Mirelle had been a journalist.

"Package received," Talia read from the registration confirmation on her display. "Dead-hand registered. Client: M. Expiry: seventy-two hours rolling. Node RD-14." She paused. "The first window starts now. Seventy-two hours. Miss one, nothing happens. Miss two —"

"I know the terms."

"— the package goes where you told it to go and I never see the addresses and I never know what happened and as far as my records are concerned, I stored a data cache for a client who stopped checking in." Talia turned from the display. "That's the service. No sentiment. No follow-up. No posthumous investigation. I'm a node, not a mourner."

"I'm not asking you to mourn."

"Good. I'm expensive and bad at it." She picked up her mug. The tea had gone cold. She drank it anyway. "Anything else?"

"Is there anything crossing your node I should know about? Sump-adjacent. Infrastructure. NitroCore classifications."

Talia's expression didn't change. But the luminescent ring pulsed — once, slow — and Mirelle recognized that pulse. She'd seen it in their previous transactions, the handful of times she'd bought data from this node, always small purchases, always specific, always paid for in information or in favors she'd rather not have owed. The pulse meant Talia was deciding what to sell her.

"There's a classification upgrade on seven Sump-adjacent conduit junctions," Talia said. "Effective next quarter. Maintenance access reclassified from municipal to restricted-corporate. The authorization chain moves from local supervisors to NitroCore's regional infrastructure directorate."

"Which junctions?"

Talia named them. Three of the seven were on Mirelle's map — junctions within two hundred meters of disappearance sites.

"The price?"

"Free." Talia set down the mug. "I profit from what you do with it. You publish, markets move, my other clients get nervous, prices go up. The chaos you create is good for business." She paused. "The data you just gave me is worth more than the dead-hand fee. Consider the junction list a receipt."

Mirelle didn't thank her. Talia didn't expect thanks. The transaction was complete — the architecture built, the failsafe registered, the price paid.

She picked up her stylus and put it in her pocket.

"Seventy-two hours," Talia said.

"Seventy-two hours."

Mirelle walked out through the repair shop. The woman at the counter didn't look up.

---

The Resonance District was louder at street level than it had been inside Talia's node. The insulation had done its work — the transition from the node's attenuated hum to the district's full-spectrum vibration was like stepping from a sealed room into open water. Mirelle felt it in her jaw, her sternum, the ringing in her right ear that spiked and then settled into the constant high tone she'd been carrying for three weeks.

She walked north. Back toward the Sector 3 commercial strip, but not the same route — Variation C, the return leg, designed to avoid retracing her approach. Through the market-adjacent streets where the Hum Market's commerce spilled into the surrounding corridors — vendors selling ampoules, frame components, counter-surveillance tools, all under the orange glow that was deeper here, more saturated, the light of pipes that had been carrying nitro since before the Sump was the Sump.

Her coat was lighter. The jacket pocket empty now — the mirror drive with Talia. Thirty-two sheets of paper still in the lining, the first drive still in her boot. The data she'd given Talia was identical to the data she was carrying, held now by someone whose business model depended on keeping it intact.

Sixteen names. Five sectors. A geographic correlation that any competent analyst could attribute to proximity bias. But Talia had said *that's a pattern* first, before she'd said anything else, and Talia's professional interest was not easy to earn.

She thought about Gauthier. *What do you actually have?* She had more now. She had the junction reclassifications — seven conduit junctions moving from municipal to restricted-corporate next quarter. Three of them on her map. That wasn't anecdotal. That was NitroCore restructuring access to the same locations where workers had disappeared, and the restructuring hadn't been announced publicly, and the timing was the kind of thing that made patterns into stories.

She needed to get inside those junctions before the reclassification took effect. Before restricted-corporate access meant biometric clearance levels she couldn't borrow or steal. She had weeks. Maybe less.

The tolerance bands were widening. The Feed was reclassifying. The access was being locked down — not because something was wrong but because the definition of wrong was being adjusted to accommodate whatever was happening, and Mirelle was watching the adjustment in real time and documenting it on recycled paper because that was the only medium that didn't exist on any mesh.

She reached the Sector 3 commercial strip. The crowd absorbed her — second shift ending, third shift beginning, the Sump's metabolism cycling workers through its corridors the way the conduit network cycled nitro through its pipes. She moved with the current. Unremarkable. Her frame running the visible layer that said *Sump resident, textile sector, credential tier Basic* while the private partition recorded nothing and the implant behind her left eye stored the route home in local memory.

A feed-screen scrolled above the transit stairs. Weather. Transit advisory. Employment listings.

And between them, in the same font, at the same scroll speed:

**PERSONNEL UPDATE: Conduit maintenance restructuring continues across five sectors. All affected personnel reassigned. No disruption to service expected. — NitroCore Sump Division**

*Five sectors.* The language was expanding. When she'd started, the Feed notices had been local — single junctions, individual crew restructurings, the bureaucratic grammar of one disappearance at a time. Now it was five sectors. The reclassification was outpacing her count.

She didn't stop walking. She'd learned that eight weeks ago, outside Lien Suen's building — you don't stop in the current. You don't become the obstacle the flow routes around. You move with it and you record what you see and you keep the data on hardware that doesn't exist on any network and you check in every seventy-two hours so that the machine you've built keeps holding the weight.

The hum was in her teeth. The ringing in her right ear was steady — the new constant, the sound her body had started making in response to the sound the infrastructure made in response to whatever was happening in the trunk-lines beneath the Resonance District where six first-generation conduit lines converged at the highest-throughput junction in the city and the readings were above thirty and the people who lived on top of it called the sound *normal* because they'd never heard anything else.

She climbed the transit stairs toward the brightline. The orange glow thinned as she ascended — conduit light giving way to the filtered white of the Mid-Levels, the architectural boundary where the Sump ended and the city above it could pretend the Sump didn't exist.

She had seventy-two hours. Then she would ping the address Talia had given her, and the timer would reset, and the architecture would hold.

Seventy-two hours. Then seventy-two more.
