# Chapter 16

## Private Log

> *"We do not ask you to believe us. We ask you to count. Count the names. Count the dates. Count the readings. Then ask yourself what kind of system requires you to stop counting."*
>
> — *The Kindling Letters*, Vol. III

---nn## Draft v1

The log was not a log.

It was a file nested inside the maintenance-scheduling partition of his service-issue frame — the partition nobody audited because it contained shift rosters and gasket replacement timelines and the accumulated clerical debris of six years of trunk-line inspections that no supervisor had ever opened and no NitroCore data sweep had ever flagged. Fuxi had created it eleven weeks ago. He had given it a filename that looked like a parts requisition — *REQ-4E-GASKET-BATCH-2175-Q3.dat* — and he updated it at the end of every shift, sitting at station 3 in the monitoring bay while the automated systems uploaded the day's readings and Chen Wei powered down his screens with the same sequence of keystrokes he had used for twenty years.

Eleven weeks. Fifty-three entries. Each one a timestamp, an RCI reading, and a decay profile — the numbers the official logs captured, plus the thing the official logs didn't: the *shape* of each correction. Whether the decline from peak to baseline followed the expected logarithmic curve, the messy asymptotic approach of a physical system settling through friction and redundancy. Or whether it was something else.

Linear. Clean. Deliberate.

He had started the log after the third spike.

The first had been the one eleven weeks and four days ago: monitor 6, peak of 30.8, linear descent, twenty-six seconds. Not the highest reading he'd seen — there had been an earlier spike, months back, the one Chen Wei had dismissed as a fluctuation. But that one had entered the official system, aged through the active queue, and been archived. Gone. This one was different because Fuxi was different — because the earlier spike had lodged in his body like a splinter, and when the second one came he was watching for the shape. The second had come nine days later — monitor 6 again, peak of 31.2, linear descent, twenty-two seconds. Faster. The third had come fourteen days after that, and by then Fuxi had stopped believing that the word *fluctuation* contained enough information to describe what was happening.

The third spike was when he started the file.

He sat now at station 3, the shift's data uploading to the grid management system, and opened the parts-requisition file on his cracked frame while the amber light of the monitoring bay turned his hands the same orange as everything else below the Mid-Levels. The file rendered in the standard service text — monospaced, low-resolution, designed for inventory tracking. Each entry was a row. Each row was a shift.

Fifty-three rows.

Not all of them contained spikes. The trunk-line ran clean for days at a stretch — baseline 26 to 28, the steady resonance of nitro moving through first-generation infrastructure at three times its design specification. Normal. The hum constant. The monitors green. Then a spike would come — not on a schedule, not in a pattern Fuxi could predict, but with a frequency that was increasing. In the first four weeks of the log, he'd recorded three anomalous readings. In the last four weeks, seven. The spikes were getting more frequent, and the peaks were climbing — 30.8, 31.2, 31.5, and last week a reading that had touched 32.1 before the linear correction pulled it back to baseline in nineteen seconds.

The corrections were getting faster too. The first linear descent had taken forty seconds. The most recent had taken nineteen. As if whatever was correcting the reading was getting better at it. As if it was *practicing.*

Fuxi scrolled to the bottom of the file and added today's entry. No spike. Baseline throughout. He typed the date, the shift start and end times, the high and low RCI readings, the ambient temperature in the monitoring bay, and the note he added to every entry regardless of whether anything had happened: *Decay profile: N/A. No anomalous reading this shift.*

Then he opened the second section of the file.

This section had no header. No formatting. Just dates and names — the dates copied from the municipal residential advisory that updated on his frame every seventy-two hours, and the names gathered from the corridor. Not the advisory itself, which never contained names. The advisory said things like: *Residential unit 14-7B: vacancy logged. Residential unit 14-3A: vacancy logged. Residential unit 9-12C: vacancy logged.* Vacancy. As if people had moved. As if they had packed their things and walked to the lift and ascended to the Mid-Levels or descended further into the Deep Sump or done anything other than the thing that the advisory's language was designed to make invisible.

Fuxi did not know what had happened to the people in 14-7B and 14-3A and 9-12C. Nobody did. That was the architecture of a vacancy — it was the absence of information shaped like the absence of a person. One day the corridor lights were on behind a frosted polymer door. The next day they were off. The neighbours said *they moved* or *they went to family* or *I think they transferred,* and the advisory said *vacancy logged,* and the shift continued and the hum continued and the trunk-lines carried their cargo and the monitors stayed green.

But Fuxi had the dates. The advisory updated every seventy-two hours, and the vacancy logs had timestamps, and the timestamps could be matched against the entries in the first section of his file.

He had matched them.

Not tonight. Weeks ago. The night after the fifth spike, sitting on the blue textile in the apartment with Nuwa asleep and the conduit glow pulsing through the frosted polymer window, he had opened both sections of the file side by side on the cracked frame display and looked at the numbers.

The correlation was not clean. It was not a one-to-one alignment — spike here, vacancy there, line drawn between them. The world did not work like that. The world worked in noise and approximation and the accumulated mess of systems interacting with other systems in ways that nobody fully mapped. But the correlation was there. Each anomalous RCI spike on monitor 6 — the linear ones, the ones that self-corrected with a precision that physical systems did not possess — fell within forty-eight to seventy-two hours of a vacancy logged in the residential blocks closest to the Resonance District boundary. Not every vacancy had a spike. But every spike had a vacancy.

Every spike had a vacancy.

He had checked it three times. He had reordered the data by date, by block number, by RCI peak value. He had looked for confounders — throughput changes, scheduled maintenance, demand cycles that could explain both the readings and the timing. He had found none. The throughput logs showed nothing unusual. The maintenance schedules were routine. The demand cycles followed their quarterly pattern, and the spikes did not.

The spikes followed something else.

Fuxi closed the file. The upload chime sounded — the shift's data had been transmitted. The monitoring bay screens showed their post-upload confirmation, amber text on amber background, and Chen Wei was already standing, pulling his jacket from the hook, moving through the end-of-shift sequence with the automatism of a man who had performed it seven thousand times and would perform it seven thousand more.

"Quiet shift," Chen Wei said.

"Quiet shift."

Chen Wei nodded. That was the exchange. The daily confirmation that nothing had happened, that the trunk-lines had held, that the monitors had stayed green, that the system had done what the system was designed to do. Chen Wei left. Fuxi heard his boots on the grating, the sound diminishing down the corridor toward the ascent shaft. Then silence — not true silence, never true silence in the Deep Sump, but the relative silence of a monitoring bay after shift change, when the automated systems ran alone and the hum was the only presence.

Fuxi sat for a moment longer. The hum pressed against his sternum. The orange glow turned his hands to instruments of the infrastructure — orange skin, orange nails, the fine dust that settled in the creases of his knuckles and the lines of his palms and that he carried home every night despite the mat. He thought about the file. About the columns of dates and readings and vacancies that sat inside a gasket requisition on a cracked frame in the maintenance-scheduling partition that nobody audited.

He thought about what the file meant.

Not what it proved — it proved nothing. Correlation was not causation. He had heard this phrase in the quarterly safety briefings that NitroCore mandated and the municipal service attended and nobody believed and everybody signed. *Correlation is not causation.* A statistical relationship between two variables does not establish that one produces the other. The spikes and the vacancies could be coincidental. They could be products of a shared underlying cause — increased throughput generating both RCI fluctuations and the conditions that made people leave. They could be noise. They could be the kind of pattern the human brain was evolved to find in random data — the face in the clouds, the signal in the static, the meaning in the meaningless.

But the decay profiles were linear.

Systems didn't do that. Fuxi had maintained trunk-lines for six years. He had watched thousands of fluctuations spike and settle. He knew what a self-correcting system looked like — the oscillation, the overshoot, the messy asymptotic approach. He knew it in his body the way he knew the feel of a properly seated gasket and the sound of a conduit running at spec and the vibration frequency of a trunk-line carrying R1 nitro at peak throughput. Physical systems decayed through friction. They did not draw straight lines from peak to baseline. They did not arrive at the target in nineteen seconds and stop.

Something was correcting those readings. Not the system's redundancy margins. Not the flow regulators. Something that knew what baseline was and chose to return to it with the efficiency of a hand reaching for a switch.

Fuxi stood. Pulled his jacket from the hook. The reflective strips were peeling worse now — the left shoulder strip had detached entirely, and the zipper still stuck at the midpoint. He had stopped filing for replacements.

---

The apartment smelled like broth.

Nuwa was at the heating element, her back to the door, sleeves pushed to her elbows. The violet staining on her forearms had darkened — five months of chemical solvent exposure accumulating in the skin like a record of shifts worked and safety requisitions unfiled and protective equipment that existed in the plant manager's spreadsheet but not on Nuwa's hands. She was stirring something with the concentration she gave to everything: precise, efficient, present.

"Boots," she said.

He stepped onto the mat. Pulled them off. The routine was the same — the mat, the boots, the cold concrete through his socks, the hum in the walls transmitting the conduit network's pulse into the bones of the building. Home frequency.

"I got it," she said, without turning around.

"Got what."

She turned. Her face was doing the thing it did when she had built a case and was waiting for the right moment to present it — the controlled neutrality that preceded the layered argument, each reason stacked precisely to support the next. But tonight there was something else underneath. Something that looked, from the angle where Fuxi stood in his socks on the cold floor of their apartment in the Sump of Neo-Shanghai, like happiness.

"The P-3."

She held up her left arm. The frame was new. Not refurbished-new — the housing was the same matte grey of a Shenlong factory unit, but the edges were clean, the screen uncracked, and the AR overlay that pulsed once in his peripheral vision when she activated it was sharp and stable and free of the artifacts that had plagued her salvaged unit.

"Stall 14," she said. "He held it. Five months. I think he felt sorry for me. Or he couldn't find another buyer. Either way."

Fuxi looked at the frame on her wrist. Five months of savings. Five months of subsidized rations and double shifts and the math that Nuwa had run forward and backward and sideways until the numbers had agreed to cooperate. Five months of the plan — *their* plan, the architecture of small, accumulated sacrifices that was supposed to open the door to the Mid-Level transfer, the QC positions at Yuen's plant, the employer-sponsored transit permit, the forty meters of altitude that measured the distance between the Sump and something less than the Sump.

"The sensory filter?" he asked.

"Works. I tested it on the walk home. Walked past the junction on level 2 — the one that usually scrambles the overlay. Nothing. Clean signal. Full AR." She turned back to the heating element. "My supervisor is going to look like a complete person for the first time in six months."

He almost smiled. The way he almost smiled — the compression, the containment, the expression that reached the muscles of his face and stopped before it arrived at the surface. Not because the monitoring bay was watching. Because the habit of containment had followed him home and settled into his face the way the orange dust settled into the creases of his hands.

Her shoulders had dropped two centimetres. Her jaw had unclenched. She moved through the apartment without the low-grade calculation that usually governed her steps — the unconscious economizing of a body that had learned to spend nothing it didn't have to. She had the frame. The plan was working. The next step was the transfer application — Nuwa had the paperwork drafted, the QC qualification timeline mapped, the transit permit pathway identified. She had built a structure out of the narrow materials available to a woman in the Sump with violet-stained hands and an uneven haircut and a mind that worked in architectures of opportunity. The structure was sound. The math checked.

He sat at the table. She set a bowl in front of him — broth, reconstituted protein, the green thing that might have been bok choy. Steam rose. He ate.

"The application window opens in three weeks," she said, sitting across from him with her own bowl. "Yuen's plant posts the QC positions first internally. If I apply with the P-3 already integrated — functional frame, sensory filter, full AR qualification — I'm ahead of anyone still running salvaged units. The transfer committee reviews on a thirty-day cycle. That puts the decision six weeks out. If they approve, GridLine processes the employer-sponsored transit permit in another twenty days. Two months. Two months and I'm in the Mid-Levels."

She laid it out the way she always laid things out — the bricks, the structure, the pathway rendered in precise steps with precise timelines and the quiet certainty of someone who had done the math so many times that the numbers had become load-bearing.

Fuxi ate and listened and thought about the file.

About the vacancy logged in block 14, unit 7B, sixteen days ago. He knew the tenant — not well, not as a friend, but as a face in the corridor. A man named Guo who worked the water recycling station on level 1. Guo had a loud laugh and a daughter who played in the corridor and a shift pattern that overlapped with Fuxi's ascent from the Deep Sump, so that they passed each other three times a week at the lift doors, Guo going down and Fuxi going up, and the nod between them was the nod of people who shared an infrastructure — the same corridor, the same hum, the same orange glow through the same frosted polymer windows.

Guo's door had been dark for sixteen days. The advisory had said *vacancy logged.* The daughter was not in the corridor. Nobody had said *shimmer.* Nobody had said anything. The absence had the texture of all the absences in the Sump — a silence that occupied the space where a person had been, bounded by the walls of not-asking and not-saying and the municipal advisory's relentless, functional euphemism.

Sixteen days ago, monitor 6 had spiked to 31.5. Linear descent. Twenty-two seconds.

Fuxi ate his broth.

"You're quiet," Nuwa said.

"Standard."

"Quieter than standard." She studied him across the table. The conduit glow came through the frosted polymer window and mixed with the overhead fixture she'd repaired — the light in the apartment was orange and white, and it turned her face into the study in warmth that he remembered from a hundred shared meals and that he was, right now, in this moment, memorizing. Not because he was afraid. Because the file had taught him to count, and counting had taught him to notice, and noticing had made the ordinary things — Nuwa's face, Nuwa's hands, the bowl of broth, the blue textile on the bed, the hum in the walls — heavier. More present. The way objects gained weight when you understood they could be taken.

"Long shift," he said.

She accepted it. Not because she believed him — Nuwa's acceptance was never credulity. It was a choice. The same choice she had made when she said *normal crowd* and he said *normal crowd* and neither of them named the shimmer near the Hum Market. The architecture of well-intentioned silence. He lived inside it. He maintained it. He maintained it the way he maintained the trunk-lines — not because he believed the system was sound, but because the alternative to maintenance was a question he couldn't answer while his sister needed five more weeks.

No. Two months. Two months for the transfer. Two months of the plan working. Two months of Nuwa rising — forty meters, a different plant, better medical, a frame that worked — and him staying in the Deep Sump where the monitors showed what the monitors showed and the file grew by one entry every shift.

He would not tell her about the file.

This was not the old silence — the mutual avoidance, the shared agreement to keep certain observations inside the body. This was different. This was Fuxi holding information that Nuwa did not have and choosing not to give it to her, because giving it to her would make the plan impossible. You could not save for a frame and plan a transfer and build a future forty meters above the Sump while also knowing that the trunk-lines beneath your feet were spiking in correlation with your neighbours going dark. You could not carry both architectures — the architecture of rising and the architecture of counting. One of them had to be set down, and Fuxi had decided, sitting on the blue textile eleven weeks ago with the file open on his cracked frame, that the one he set down would be the one that was his.

He would carry the file. She would carry the plan. He would count. She would climb.

The division was clean. Precise. Linear.

Like a decay profile that wasn't a decay profile.

---

He found the pamphlet on the ascent shaft floor three days later.

Not *found* — the pamphlets were not hidden. They appeared in the corridors and the lift shafts and the market stalls, folded into single sheets of recycled stock that the municipal service periodically collected and the Kindling periodically replaced. Fuxi had seen hundreds of them. He had stepped over them and around them and sometimes picked them up to clear his path the way he picked up any debris in the infrastructure corridors, because debris near trunk-line access points was a maintenance issue and maintenance issues were his job.

He had never read one.

This one was different only because he was different. The pamphlet was the same — single sheet, recycled stock, printed in the Sump's universal font (the one the corridor signage used, the one every frame defaulted to, the font of infrastructure). The text was Kindling text. He recognized the formatting — the centered header, the short paragraphs, the questions that were not questions but invitations to count.

*How many vacancy advisories has your block received this quarter?*

He knew the answer. Seven.

*How many of those vacancies were transfers? How many had transit permits? How many packed their things and walked to the lift and rode it up?*

He knew the answer to that too.

*The Sump is not losing people to opportunity. The Sump is losing people. The distinction is the system's favorite silence.*

Fuxi stood in the ascent shaft with the pamphlet in his hand and the lift rumbling beneath his boots and the trunk-line hum pressing through the walls and into his sternum. He had read Kindling language before — overheard it in the corridors, seen it in the pamphlets he'd stepped over, registered it as political noise generated by a collective that dealt in grievance and rhetoric and the kind of truth that was true but not useful. He had filed it in the same mental partition where he filed the things that were not actionable: the hum's changing texture, the readings that self-corrected, the questions that formed in the back of his mind like frequencies he couldn't quite resolve.

But the pamphlet's language was not noise tonight. Tonight the language had numbers under it — his numbers, the file's numbers, the fifty-three entries and the vacancy dates and the correlation that was not proof but was not nothing. The Kindling said *the Sump is losing people.* Fuxi's file said *the trunk-lines spike before they go.* The two statements were not the same statement. But they occupied adjacent space. They fit together the way a gasket fits a housing — not by design but by the geometry of the problem, because the problem had a shape and the shape required both pieces.

*Sacrifice district.*

He had heard the phrase. Everyone in the Sump had heard it — Kindling vocabulary, political language, the kind of words that floated through the corridors the way the pamphlets floated through the lift shafts. Words that named what the advisory didn't. Words that replaced *vacancy logged* with something that had edges.

Fuxi had never used the phrase. Had never said it aloud, had never let it settle in his mouth, because Kindling language was political and political was dangerous and dangerous was the opposite of what kept Nuwa fed and housed and saving. He maintained the system. The system maintained his sister. The vocabulary of maintenance was the vocabulary of survival: *conduit inspection, RCI reading, scheduled replacement, self-correction, baseline.*

But *sacrifice district* had a precision to it that the maintenance vocabulary lacked. The maintenance vocabulary described what the system did. *Sacrifice district* described what the system was *for.* And Fuxi, standing in the ascent shaft with fifty-three entries on his cracked frame and a pamphlet in his hand, could feel the second vocabulary pressing against the first — not replacing it, not yet, but occupying the space next to it, the way a new harmonic occupies the space next to a fundamental frequency and changes the texture of the sound without changing the note.

He folded the pamphlet. Put it in his jacket pocket, next to Jun's multitool.

The lift arrived. He stepped in. Pressed the contact for Level 0. Felt the cargo lift begin its slow climb through the shaft, the trunk-lines humming on all sides, the resonance changing as he rose — the Deep Sump's bass drone giving way to the Sump's thinner, quicker composite. His body adjusted. It always adjusted. The headache eased. The copper taste faded. The daily recalibration of a man who lived between frequencies.

The pamphlet was in his pocket. The file was on his frame. The words were in his head — *sacrifice district,* two words that sounded like a technical designation, that had the weight and specificity of infrastructure vocabulary, that fit into the same grammatical slot as *conduit junction* and *trunk-line section* and *monitoring bay.* Two words that described a place. His place.

He did not use them aloud. He did not say them to Nuwa when he walked through the door and stepped onto the mat and sat at the table and ate the food she'd made and listened to the update on the transfer application — three weeks to the posting, six weeks to review, two months to the Mid-Levels — and watched her face in the orange-and-white light and carried, in his pocket and on his frame and in the space behind his sternum where the hum lived, the weight of a correlation that was not proof and a vocabulary that was not his.

Not yet.

But the old vocabulary was losing purchase. *Self-correction* was losing purchase. *Fluctuation* was losing purchase. *Baseline* was a word that meant something different now — not the reading the system returned to, but the reading something *chose* to return to, deliberately, linearly, with the precision of a hand reaching for a switch. And *vacancy logged* — the advisory's phrase, the system's phrase, the phrase that turned a disappearance into a clerical event — was a phrase that Fuxi could no longer read without hearing the Kindling's translation underneath it, the way you can't unhear a harmony once someone has pointed it out.

He sat in the apartment and listened to Nuwa talk about the future — the QC positions, the transit permits, the forty meters — and he held the file and the pamphlet and the dead man's multitool and the silence that was not mutual anymore but *his,* his choice, his architecture, the structure he was building to keep her inside the plan while he counted what the plan couldn't hold.

Outside, the conduit glow pulsed. The hum carried through the walls. The municipal advisory had been updated four times this quarter. The monitors in the Deep Sump showed green. The system was working. The system was self-correcting. The readings were within tolerance.

And in a gasket requisition file on a cracked frame in the maintenance-scheduling partition that nobody audited, fifty-three entries said that the system's corrections were too clean and its tolerances were too precise and its vacancies had timestamps that matched its spikes, and a maintenance man in the Sump of Neo-Shanghai sat with the data in his pocket and the pamphlet next to his father's tool and did not speak.

# Chapter 17

## The Back-Channel

> *"Let the record note that this framework was built not in triumph but in exhaustion. We did not agree because we were wise. We agreed because we were too tired to keep killing each other. I pray the fatigue holds."*
>
> — *Address to the Signatories* — Khalil Al-Fahim, 2044

---nn## Draft v1

The response arrived on a Tuesday.

Not with urgency — the UGC's internal document routing system did not accommodate urgency. It arrived in the queue of Zeyad's primary datapad at 09:14, slotted between a revised committee agenda for the following week's session and a personnel notice regarding the reassignment of a translator in the East Asian Liaison pool. The routing metadata indicated that the document had been processed through three departmental reviews, two classification cross-checks, and a final clearance authorization before reaching his queue. The processing time, from submission to delivery: twenty-three business days.

Thirteen days beyond the estimated window. Standard.

He opened it at his desk. The office was the same — the small room in the administrative wing, the photograph of Khalil at the corner, the pen beside the notebook, the three datapads stacked by priority. The overhead light was the same institutional white it had been for the six years he'd occupied this office. The coffee was cold. The hum was present in the floor — the building's conduit infrastructure, four stories below, transmitting the frequency of a civilization into the marble and steel of the institution that was supposed to govern it.

The document was titled: *Response to Data Request — Ref: AF-2175-0041 — Arctic Research Corridor, Station 7.*

Fourteen pages. He had requested sensor logs, VEC preliminary assessment, and classification routing documentation. The response contained none of these. What it contained was a summary — compiled by the Classification Directorate's Review Section, formatted in the standard institutional template, structured with the headers and subheaders and cross-reference markers that Zeyad could read the way other people read faces.

The summary told him nothing.

Not nothing in the colloquial sense — not "little" or "less than expected." Nothing. The document was an architecture of absence dressed in institutional language. Page one: acknowledgment of the request, procedural citation, confirmation that the Classification Directorate had reviewed the materials referenced. Page two: scope determination — "The materials referenced fall within the classification parameters established under GCTA Protocol, Annex B, and are subject to the access provisions of GCTA Classification Protocol, Annex C." Page three through six: redacted. Not blank — the formatting was preserved, the section headers visible, the paragraph numbering intact. But the content had been replaced with classification bars, the grey rectangles that indicated material removed under Annex C's provision for "data classified under security assessment whose cross-institutional distribution requires dual authorization from the Classification Directorate and the originating institutional entity."

Dual authorization. The Classification Directorate could not release the data without the VEC's consent. The VEC could not release the data without the Classification Directorate's clearance. Two locks on one door, each key held by a hand that pointed at the other.

Pages seven through ten: a precis of the Arctic-7 station's operational history — commissioning date, staffing complement, research mandate. Information Zeyad had possessed before filing the request. Publicly available. The kind of information an institution provided when it wanted the response to have weight without having content.

Pages eleven through fourteen: redacted.

He read the document twice. The second reading was slower than the first — not because he expected to find something he'd missed but because the pattern of the redaction was itself information. The grey rectangles were not random. They followed the document's structure with a precision that revealed what had been removed by the shape of what remained. The section headers that survived — "Station Configuration," "Personnel Disposition," "Environmental Assessment Summary" — indicated that the original document had contained the sensor logs and VEC assessment he'd requested. The Classification Directorate had not refused to compile the materials. It had compiled them, reviewed them, redacted the substance, and delivered the architecture.

The shell of an answer. The institutional equivalent of a status update — contained, no action required — translated into fourteen pages of formatted compliance.

Zeyad placed the datapad on the desk. Picked up the pen. Opened the notebook.

He wrote: *AF-0041 returned. 23 days. 14 pages, 8 redacted under Annex C. Sensor logs "unavailable pending ongoing assessment." VEC preliminary assessment "outside scope of current access authorization." Classification routing — the one document that would show WHO reclassified Arctic-7 from scientific to security — redacted in full.*

He paused. The pen hovered. The handwriting was steady — small, precise, the product of decades writing in margins too narrow for large script. The ink was black on cream. The notebook was leather. The pen was Khalil's.

*Annex C requires dual authorization for cross-institutional data release. Neither entity can release without the other's consent. This is not a classification error. This is a classification design. The provision exists to ensure that data requiring both VEC and GCTA review can be held indefinitely in the space between two authorizations that will never converge.*

He looked at the annotation. Five lines. Black ink. Not for the institutional record — the datapad held the formal acknowledgment of receipt, timestamped and filed. This was for the other record. The one in the drawer.

He wrote one more line: *The system is not failing to process my request. The system is processing it exactly as designed.*

The pen stopped. He sat in the small office and looked at the photograph and thought about the word *designed*, and about the thirty-four years he had spent operating within a system whose design he had studied without understanding what the design was for.

---

The channel had been in his possession for eleven days.

Not a channel he had opened. Not a channel he had requested through institutional means. It had arrived the way things arrived when the institutional channels had been exhausted — through a contact in the Mediterranean corridor, a former colleague from the refugee logistics posting who had maintained relationships with journalists and academics in the information underground. The contact had not explained how the connection worked. He had said: "There's a journalist in the Sump. French. She has data you should see. She has questions that overlap with yours." And he had given Zeyad an encrypted protocol address and a single-use authentication key and the instruction to initiate contact only from an unsecured terminal — not the UGC's monitored network, not a diplomatic comm, not any device whose traffic was routed through the institutional infrastructure that logged, timestamped, and archived every transmission.

Zeyad had not used it.

For eleven days, the protocol address had existed in two places: the contact's memory and a line in Zeyad's notebook, written in the margin of a page already filled with annotations on the Annex B classification structure. He had not transferred it to a datapad. He had not tested the connection. He had not, in the precise language of the diplomatic communication protocols he had spent his career operating within, initiated contact with an extra-institutional source through an unlogged channel.

The distinction mattered. It mattered because Zeyad Al-Fahim's professional identity was built on the conviction that the institutional record was the mechanism by which accountability was maintained, and the institutional record existed because every communication was logged, and every log was archived, and every archive was accessible to the committees and review boards whose oversight depended on the completeness of the record. The record was complete because the system captured everything. What the system did not capture did not exist — not legally, not procedurally, not in the framework that determined what the institution knew and what it could act on.

An unlogged channel was a hole in the record. A gap in the architecture of accountability. The kind of gap that Zeyad had spent four position papers arguing against when corporate entities exploited it.

He had also spent twenty-three days waiting for a data request to return as fourteen pages of formatted absence, and the formatted absence had taught him something that the position papers had not: the record was complete because the system captured everything, and the system was designed to ensure that everything it captured was insufficient.

The completeness was the problem.

He left his office at 19:40. The administrative wing was quiet — the day staff gone, the evening security rotation reduced to a single guard at the east entrance who nodded as Zeyad passed. The corridor lights were on their evening cycle, dimmer, the institutional white softened to something approaching amber. The Hall of Nations was empty. The holographic flags rippled in their perpetual non-wind. The Jordanian standard flickered.

The secure comm alcove was at the end of the east corridor, past the archive access point and the utility room that held the building's local server infrastructure. The alcove was not secure in the classified sense — it was not a SCIF, not a hardened chamber, not a space designed for the transmission of sensitive materials. It was a room with a terminal that was not connected to the UGC's institutional network. A leftover from the building's previous configuration, when the administrative wing had housed a satellite office of the Swiss cantonal government and the terminal had been used for non-governmental communications. The terminal had been disconnected from the cantonal network when the UGC expanded into the wing. It had not been decommissioned. It had been forgotten — a piece of infrastructure that existed in no inventory because it belonged to no system, and therefore occupied the specific bureaucratic lacuna that allowed Zeyad to use it without logging its use.

He sat at the terminal. The screen was grey. The interface was decades old — no holographic overlay, no AR integration, just a flat display and a physical keyboard whose keys had the stiff resistance of mechanisms that had not been pressed in years.

He entered the protocol address. The authentication key.

The connection established in four seconds. No visual feed. Text only. The encryption protocol stripped the transmission to its minimum — characters on a screen, routed through nodes that Zeyad's contact had assured him were outside institutional monitoring. Whether the assurance was accurate, Zeyad could not verify. He was operating on trust — not institutional trust, not the trust of verified credentials and diplomatic protocols, but the older, more dangerous kind. The trust of one person believing another person's word.

The cursor blinked.

He typed: *This is the contact your associate mentioned. I have questions about Arctic-7. I'm told you have data that intersects with those questions.*

Seventeen seconds. The cursor blinked.

The response appeared: *You're late. I expected you two weeks ago.*

He looked at the words on the screen. The register was not diplomatic. It was direct, compressed, stripped of the layered courtesy that governed the exchanges he was accustomed to — exchanges where "I have concerns" meant catastrophe and "I would welcome clarification" meant accusation. This was the register of someone who did not operate through institutions. Someone who said what they meant because the gap between surface and substance was a luxury they could not afford.

He typed: *I required time to evaluate whether this channel was appropriate.*

*It's not. That's why you're using it.*

The directness sat on the screen like a fact. He almost smiled — the compression, the containment, the expression that reached the muscles of his face and stopped. Not because the terminal was watching. Because the woman on the other end of this connection had, in nine words, described the contradiction he had spent eleven days not resolving.

He typed: *I have a data request response from the Classification Directorate. Fourteen pages. Eight redacted under Annex C. The sensor logs I requested are listed as "unavailable pending ongoing assessment." The VEC preliminary assessment is "outside current access authorization." The classification routing documentation — the document that would show who reclassified the station from scientific to security jurisdiction — is redacted in its entirety.*

*When did you file?*

*Twenty-three days ago. Estimated processing was ten to fifteen.*

*And what does the response tell you?*

He considered the question. Not its content — its function. She was not asking what the document contained. She was asking what the absence of content meant. The question was diagnostic. She was reading him the way he read committee chambers — testing whether the man on the other end of this channel could process institutional silence the way she processed source testimony.

He typed: *The Annex C provision requires dual authorization for cross-institutional data release. Neither the Classification Directorate nor the VEC can release without the other's consent. The provision is not a safeguard. It is a mechanism for indefinite containment of information that both entities have reason to suppress. The response was not a denial. It was a demonstration that the system is architecturally incapable of producing the information I requested through the channel I used to request it.*

Twenty-two seconds.

*You're faster than I expected. Most institutional people take months to see that.*

*I have been in this institution for thirty-four years. I have seen it before. I have not seen it applied to a research station.*

*It's not a research station anymore.*

The sentence sat on the screen. Five words. He read them three times. Not because they were ambiguous — because they were precise, and the precision implied a knowledge base that his institutional channels had not provided.

*What do you have?* he typed.

The response took forty seconds. Longer than the others. She was deciding how much to share. When it came, it was structured — not diplomatic structure but journalistic structure, the architecture of evidence arranged for comprehension rather than courtesy.

*I have eighteen confirmed disappearances across five sectors of the Neo-Shanghai Sump, spanning eleven months. Each disappearance correlates geographically with high-throughput conduit junctions — the points where nitro infrastructure operates at maximum density. I have RCI readings from eleven of those sites showing values above residential baseline. I have a correlation between the timing of anomalous trunk-line spikes and the dates of those disappearances — not one-to-one, but consistent: every spike has a vacancy within forty-eight to seventy-two hours.*

She continued: *I also have a classified Arctic-7 infrastructure assessment — pages twelve through thirty-one — that I obtained through other means. The document shows throughput density by junction. A research lead's handwritten annotation in the margins reads "co-origin." Void breach frequency and nitro throughput co-originate at the highest-density junction points. When I overlay my Sump disappearance data on the Arctic-7 junction model, the pattern matches at city scale.*

Zeyad sat at the terminal in the dim corridor and read the words on the grey screen and felt the hum through the floor — faint, distant, the New Geneva whisper of a frequency that was, according to the data now appearing on his screen, correlating with the disappearance of human beings at the points where it was loudest.

*The infrastructure was designed this way,* she typed. *Not negligence. Architecture.*

He did not type for thirty seconds. The cursor blinked. The terminal hummed with the low-grade electrical vibration of old hardware. His hands were on the keyboard — the same hands that held Khalil's pen, that touched the portrait frame, that filed the reports and drafted the motions and took the notes in the margins. The same hands that were now, for the first time in thirty-four years of diplomatic service, engaged in a communication that the institutional record would not contain.

He typed: *The GCTA briefing on Arctic-7 uses the word "contained." Military vocabulary in a research assessment. The personnel are listed as "relocated per standard protocol." The GCTA observer seat on the Accords Compliance Review has been empty for fourteen months. Three major extractors filed late in the same quarter. Environmental reports have been recycled — template identical for six consecutive quarters. The classification was rerouted from scientific to security jurisdiction at the Directorate level, which placed it beyond the oversight channel where I have standing.*

*How long have you been asking these questions?*

*Since the quarterly review. Weeks.*

*How long has the institution been not answering them?*

He looked at the question. Looked at it the way he looked at the word *contained* in the GCTA briefing — as a word that described a condition, not a moment. The institution had not started failing to answer when he filed the request. The institution had been not-answering since the classification was routed through Annex B. Since the observer seat went empty. Since the environmental reports stopped changing. The non-answer was not a response to his question. It was the question's habitat — the institutional ecosystem in which questions of this kind were received, processed, and dissolved.

*Longer than I admitted to myself,* he typed.

Nineteen seconds.

*That's the first honest thing an institutional person has said to me in seven months of asking.*

He did not know what to say to that. The diplomatic register had responses for every institutional exchange — calibrated, layered, precise. It did not have a response for a woman in a Sump he had never visited telling him that his honesty was notable because it existed. The absence of a prepared response was itself information. He was outside the register. The back-channel was not protocol. The honesty was not diplomatic.

*I need the classification routing documentation,* she typed. *The one they redacted in full. It shows who authorized the reclassification. That's the signature that connects the institutional architecture to the operational decision. Without it, I have a pattern. With it, I have a chain of command.*

*I cannot obtain it through the channels available to me.*

*I know. That's not why I'm telling you. I'm telling you so that you understand what you're looking at. You have the institutional view — the classification anomaly, the procedural routing, the Annex C architecture. I have the ground view — the disappearances, the correlation, the infrastructure design. Neither of us has the full picture. But the fragments are the same shape.*

The same shape. He looked at the words and thought about the notebook in the drawer and the redacted pages and the pen that wrote in both records — the institutional and the secret — and the distance between the two records that had, tonight, narrowed to the width of a text cursor on a grey screen.

*What happens to this exchange?* he typed.

*On my end, nothing. Encrypted, routed through non-institutional nodes, no log. The protocol strips metadata. When this session ends, the text exists only in our memories.*

*And on my end?*

*That's your question to answer. You're the institutional man. I'm the journalist in the Sump. We both know which of us the institution protects.*

---

The corridor was empty when he stood.

The terminal screen had gone grey — the session ended, the encryption protocol purging the buffer, the connection dissolved into the electronic noise of a building whose institutional network had never registered its existence. The alcove was dark except for the standby light on the terminal's power supply, a small green dot in the dimness that pulsed at a frequency Zeyad could not consciously identify but that his body registered as present.

He walked back to his office. The Hall of Nations was empty. The flags rippled. The Jordanian standard flickered. The portrait of Khalil was a darker rectangle in the alcove — visible by the ambient light of the holographic displays, the expression on the old man's face unreadable at this distance.

Zeyad sat at his desk. The photograph. The pen. The notebook.

He opened the notebook. Found the page where the protocol address sat in the margin. Below it, he wrote:

*First exchange. She has field data — disappearances, RCI correlations, infrastructure-level evidence of designed harm. I have institutional data — classification anomalies, procedural architecture, the Annex C mechanism. Neither set is complete. Together, they form the outline of a system functioning as designed.*

He paused. The pen hovered.

*I did not log this exchange.*

Six words. The most significant six words he had written in thirty-four years of diplomatic service. Not because of what they described — back-channel communications were as old as diplomacy itself, and every experienced diplomat maintained relationships that operated in the space between formal and informal. But because Zeyad had spent his entire career arguing that the space between formal and informal was the space where accountability died, and that the institutional record existed to close that space, and that a diplomat who withheld from the record was a diplomat who had decided that the record was insufficient.

He had decided the record was insufficient.

The pen wrote: *Annex C is not a classification error. It is a classification architecture. The dual authorization provision ensures that data implicating both the VEC and the corporate extractors can be held in perpetual review, accessible to neither the oversight body (UGC) nor the public. The provision does not fail. It performs. The performance is containment.*

He closed the notebook. Placed it in the drawer — beside the photograph, beneath the stack of briefings, next to the fourteen-page response that had taken twenty-three days to deliver nothing. The drawer was becoming an archive. Not the institutional archive that preserved the record for accountability. A different archive. One that preserved what the institutional archive was designed to exclude.

He placed the pen beside the notebook. Khalil's pen. The pen that had signed the Accords — or its descendant, the mechanism identical, the ink refreshed, the metal worn smooth by four generations of hands that believed the record mattered.

The pen had written in both records tonight. The institutional acknowledgment of receipt — timestamped, filed, archived. And the notebook entry that would never enter the institutional pipeline — the exchange, the data, the six words that separated the diplomat he had been this morning from the diplomat he was now.

The hum pressed through the floor. Faint. The New Geneva whisper. The frequency of the infrastructure his great-grandfather had helped to govern, transmitted through the building where his family's legacy was displayed under glass, felt in the bones of a man who had just committed his first act of institutional disloyalty and called it what the Accords had always called the pursuit of transparency: necessary.

He turned off the desk lamp. The office went dark except for the datapad's standby light and the faint glow from the corridor through the frosted glass panel in the door. He did not go home. He sat in the dark and listened to the hum — the rumor of a frequency that was, somewhere in a city he had never visited, correlating with the disappearance of people whose names appeared in no institutional record he could access.

The practiced smile was not on his face. There was nobody to perform for. The face beneath it was the face Khalil had worn in the photograph — not triumph, not defeat. The face of a man who had signed something imperfect because the alternative was worse, and who was now, 131 years later, represented by a descendant sitting in the dark with a notebook full of things the institution would never see and a pen that had written in both records and a question that the system was architecturally incapable of answering:

What happens when the record-keeper discovers that the record is designed to be incomplete?

The flag was still flickering. He couldn't see it from here. He knew.

# Chapter 18

## Signal

> *"The earliest known record of structured auditory phenomena in mage subjects dates to 2109. It was filed as a warranty claim."*
>
> — *A History of Silence*

---nn## Chapter Brief

**Plan Confirmed:** 2026-02-11
**Divergences Noted:** None — Ch 10 seeds carried forward
**Author Notes:** Lumina: nightly 40mg routine; extra 15mg bump crept from once/week to twice. She still thinks she's in control. Dialogue heavier okay. Keep revelations LIGHT — she's only beginning to assemble the pattern, not solving the mystery. Pause before audit for author revision.

## Draft v1

The fingertips came and went.

Not numb exactly — *absent*. As if the nerve endings had decided, independently and without consulting the rest of her, to stop reporting. It happened mid-stream now, three or four times a session, a quiet dropout in sensation that lasted two or three seconds and then returned as if nothing had happened. Her left hand would go flat on the desk — not a flinch, not a tell, just a hand resting on a surface the way anyone's hand might rest on a surface — and then the feeling would come back and she'd pick up the controller and keep talking and chat wouldn't notice because chat never noticed and that was the whole point.

She noticed.

She noticed the way she noticed everything her body did wrong — a beat behind the event, after the performance had already covered it, the delayed report arriving like a memo from a department she'd stopped funding. *That happened again. Third time this stream. It's getting more frequent.* She filed it. She filed everything. The filing was the coping mechanism — categorize, shelve, move on. If the body's complaints were just data points in a log she wasn't going to read, they couldn't become a pattern she'd have to think about.

The stream ended at its usual hour. She raided Mako again — Mako was always live, Mako was a machine — and said the words she always said, the warm ones, the genuine ones, the ones that cost her something she couldn't name. Love you. Bye. Go. Get out.

Eleven seconds.

The performer left. The posture collapsed. She pulled her knees up and became small in the chair and the ring light was still on and the LED strip was still glowing and she sat in the silence that landed after every broadcast like a note released after being held too long.

Tuesday. The forty was every night — had been for fourteen months, since the titration settled. After stream. Before bed. She didn't think about it the way she didn't think about locking the door. Part of the shutdown. Part of the routine. You didn't count how often you brushed your teeth.

The bump was newer. Fifteen milligrams, on the nights the quiet room wasn't quiet enough. It had been a once-a-week thing — a bad stream, a rough episode, the kind of night where the hum leaked through and the forty wasn't enough to hold the walls. Now it was twice a week. Maybe three times last week, but two of those were back-to-back stream days and the episodes had been worse so that didn't count. She was in control. She was always in control.

She went to the bathroom. Kit behind the mirror. Scale, vial, straw. Forty milligrams. The cold burn. The subtraction.

The quiet room.

She cleaned the straw, zipped the case, put it back. Crossed to the couch — not the streaming chair, the couch, the one buried under laundry that she'd cleared a Kira-sized space in three days ago and hadn't re-cleared since. She pulled the blanket over her legs and opened her left eye's feed — not chat, not the post-stream analytics, but the private message queue that had been pulsing at the edge of her HUD for the last four hours.

She'd been ignoring it. She'd been ignoring it the way she'd been ignoring Priya's message for weeks — not deleting, not opening, just letting the notification sit in her peripheral vision like a piece of furniture she'd learned to walk around. The group chat had moved on. Dex posted memes. Tomás complained about São Paulo's transit system. Suki sent terse one-line updates from deployment that read like poetry if you squinted. Normal. The texture of people who'd known each other since they were children.

Priya hadn't brought it up again. That was worse than if she had.

---

The private messages weren't from the group chat.

Four of them. Staggered across the last ten days, from mages she knew by name but not by habit — Academy contacts, people she'd met at conferences or through the streamer circuit, the kind of connections that existed in the space between strangers and friends. Not her people. Not the group chat. These were mages who'd found her through the network the way signals find antennas — because she was visible, because she was famous, because two hundred thousand followers meant that when a mage needed someone who might *understand*, Kira Calloway was the name that came up.

She opened the first one. Ren Matsuda — Kyoto program, graduated two years ahead of her, field-certified but working research now. She'd met him once at a Varma guest lecture. Quiet. Serious. The kind of mage who documented everything.

*Kira — sorry for the cold message. I don't know who else to ask. During the Neo-Shanghai incursion three weeks ago (the Mid-Levels one, containment unit deployed), I was monitoring remotely from Kyoto. Standard observation protocol — implant tuned to atmospheric resonance, passive mode. At 11:28 UTC my R3 registered a signal I've never encountered. Not the usual ambient noise. Not the hum. Something with structure. It repeated four times at what felt like regular intervals before the incursion was contained. I ran a self-diagnostic afterward — implant nominal. I filed it as anomalous and moved on. Then I heard from two others who were monitoring the same event. They felt it too. Same timestamp. Same structure. I don't know what to do with this. I thought you might.*

She read it twice. The Lumina was working — the quiet room held, the pattern-seeking machinery was still, the part of her brain that wanted to reach for the data and *pull* was resting. She could read this and not react. She could read this and file it.

She opened the second message. Lena Okafor — Lagos program, active deployment, someone Kira had interviewed on stream two years ago about field conditions. Direct. No preamble.

*K — weird one. You know how the hum changes during incursions? Mine did something different last month. During containment ops in the Accra District corridor, my implant picked up what I can only describe as a pattern. Not the usual spike-and-fade. A repeating sequence. Like something was trying to — I don't know. Transmit? That sounds insane. Forget I said that. But the sequence repeated. Three times. Same intervals. My squad lead logged it as resonance feedback. I don't think that's what it was.*

The third was shorter. Yuki Tanaka — Osaka, field mage, someone Kira had never spoken to directly but who followed her stream.

*Calloway-san — I experienced something during the Neo-Shanghai event that I cannot reconcile with my training. My implant registered structured input during the incursion window. Not random. Structured. I have been reluctant to report it through official channels because the Academy's position on structured auditory phenomena is clear. I am contacting you because your stream discussion of deployment schedules suggested you might be open to unofficial conversation.*

The fourth was a voice message — audio only, thirty-one seconds. A man she didn't recognize, identifier stripped, routing through an anonymized relay. His voice was steady in the way that voices are steady when the person behind them is trying very hard not to sound afraid.

*"I don't know if you'll get this. I'm — I was monitoring during the Mid-Levels event. The one three weeks ago. My implant — look, I've been doing this for nine years and I've never felt anything like it. It wasn't noise. It was organized. I timed it — four repetitions, approximately ninety seconds apart. The intervals were consistent. I don't know what that means. The official line is resonance feedback. It's not resonance feedback. I know what resonance feedback feels like. This was something else. Please don't share this. I just needed someone to know."*

She played it twice. Then a third time, because her left eye had auto-transcribed it and the transcription was clean and the words on the screen were the same words she'd just heard and reading them was different from hearing them — reading them made them data, made them text, made them something she could scroll past. Hearing the voice made them a person.

She closed the message queue.

---

The apartment was dark. The ring light was still on — she should turn it off, she never turned it off — and the LED strip cast its blue-to-pink gradient across the ceiling in a soft wash that made the room look like it was underwater. She pulled the blanket tighter. The Lumina was holding. The quiet room was quiet. She didn't have to think about this.

Her left eye pulsed. The group chat.

Dex: *anyone else get that Academy health bulletin? "Structured auditory phenomena are artifacts of implant resonance feedback, not external communication." Very reassuring. Very normal thing to send unprompted to the entire mage registry.*

Priya: *I saw it. Interesting timing.*

Tomás: *what's "structured auditory phenomena"?*

Dex: *it's when your spine plays music and the Academy says it's your fault*

Tomás: *💀💀*

Priya: *It's when multiple mages report the same signal during the same event and the institution responds with a press release instead of an investigation.*

Dex: *damn Priya woke up and chose violence*

Suki: *The bulletin is standard. They issue them after any incursion with widespread implant activation. It's protocol.*

Priya: *Suki. Respectfully. When have they ever used the word "structured" in a health bulletin before?*

Suki didn't respond to that.

Kira read the exchange twice. The Lumina was holding — the room was quiet, the machinery was still — but the quiet room had a window now and through the window she could see the shape of something she didn't want to look at. Not clearly. Not the whole thing. Just the edge. The Academy had sent a health bulletin specifically addressing structured auditory phenomena. Which meant enough mages had reported it that the institution felt the need to respond. Which meant the four messages in her private queue weren't anomalies. They were a sample.

She touched the back of her neck. The hum was there. It was always there. But the thickness that had started weeks ago — the splitting, the harmonics she couldn't resolve — was different now. Not louder. Not thicker. *Tighter*. As if the chord had been retuned and the overtones were no longer bleeding into each other but aligning. Organizing. She didn't have a word for what the difference was. She had a feeling — a sensation in the bone where the implant sat, a quality of vibration that she'd been carrying for weeks now without examining because examining it meant —

She pulled the blanket over her shoulders. Drew her knees up. Became small.

The group chat had moved on. Dex was posting a clip of someone's cat walking across a keyboard during a stream. Tomás was rating the cat's content strategy. Normal. Warm. The texture of people being people.

Priya sent a private message. Not to the group. To Kira.

*I know you saw my message three weeks ago. I know you felt it too. You don't have to say anything. But I need you to know: two other mages contacted me after that night. All Academy. All describing the same thing. Structured. Repeating. During incursions. The Academy just sent a bulletin telling us it's resonance feedback. It's not resonance feedback, Kira. You know it's not.*

---

She sat with it.

The Lumina was holding — the quiet room was still quiet, the edges were still pushed back, the forty milligrams was doing what forty milligrams did. But the data was assembling itself anyway. Not because the pattern-seeking machinery had broken through the chemical barrier. Because the pattern was simple enough that she didn't need the machinery.

Priya's pull. 11:30 UTC. Her scream. Same timestamp.

Four private messages. Different mages, different locations, same event. Structured signal. Repeating intervals. Approximately ninety seconds.

The Academy health bulletin. "Structured auditory phenomena are artifacts of implant resonance feedback, not external communication." Sent to the entire mage registry. Unprompted. After enough mages reported something that the institution felt the need to define what it wasn't.

She didn't need to be a pattern-seeker to see this. She just needed to be a person who could count.

Her fingers were doing the thing — the silent chord shapes on the blanket, pressing into the fabric, finding progressions she hadn't consciously chosen. D minor. A diminished. G suspended. The fingers knew something her mind hadn't assembled yet. The fingers always knew first. That was the implant's gift — or its curse, depending on whether you believed the interface was translating sensation into music or music into sensation or whether the distinction mattered at all when your spine had been wired to a frequency you couldn't turn off since you were ten.

She opened Ren's message again. Read it a third time. *Something with structure. It repeated four times at what felt like regular intervals.*

Lena's: *A repeating sequence. Like something was trying to — I don't know. Transmit?*

The anonymous voice: *Four repetitions, approximately ninety seconds apart. The intervals were consistent.*

She didn't know what it meant. She wasn't going to pretend she did. She didn't have training for this — the Academy had taught her to suppress the scream, not to analyze it. She was a twenty-year-old streamer with numb fingertips and a nightly forty milligrams and a hum in her spine that was getting tighter, and she didn't know what *tighter* meant except that it wasn't what it used to be and the people who were supposed to explain it were sending health bulletins instead of answers.

But she could count.

Four messages in her inbox. Two more who'd contacted Priya. Priya herself. Her.

However she counted it, it wasn't an anomaly.

She stared at the ceiling. The blue-to-pink gradient shifted slowly — the LED strip's default cycle, sixty seconds per transition, the same ambient loop she'd installed three years ago and never changed. The light moved across the ceiling the way the hum moved through her spine — constant, cyclical, so familiar it had become invisible until something changed its quality and the familiarity cracked.

The Academy said it was resonance feedback. The Academy had trained her to suppress the scream at fourteen — *control is silence, if they can't hear it, it isn't happening*. The Academy had fitted the implant at ten while everyone smiled. The Academy had opinions about everything and the opinions were always the same opinion: that whatever the mages felt was the mages' problem, generated internally, managed individually, and definitely, certainly, absolutely not coming from somewhere else.

She didn't know if it was coming from somewhere else. She didn't know enough to know that. But she knew what resonance feedback felt like — she'd been living with it for a decade — and the thing in her spine wasn't that. The tightening. The alignment. The sense that the chord was resolving toward something she couldn't hear yet but could feel in the bone.

Not resonance feedback. Something else.

She wasn't going to figure out what. Not tonight. Not with the forty holding the edges back and the quiet room intact and the part of her that wanted to *reach* for the data resting. She was going to sleep. She was going to stream tomorrow. She was going to maintain the schedule and maintain the performance and maintain the line between using it and needing it that she'd been standing on since the titration settled, and she was still on the right side, she was certain, she was *almost* certain, because the forty was just the forty and the fifteen was only twice a week and she was fine.

She was fine.

She opened Ren's message. Typed:

*I hear you. I don't know what it means yet either. But you're not the only one. Can I share what you told me — anonymized — with the others who reached out?*

Sent.

Opened Lena's message. Typed the same thing, adjusted for Lena's directness:

*Got your message. Others have reported the same thing. Same structure, same intervals, same event. I'm trying to figure out if this is bigger than anecdotal. Can I connect your account with the others? No names unless you say so.*

Sent.

She copied the essential elements into a note to Yuki. More formal, matching the register:

*Tanaka-san — thank you for reaching out. I can confirm that your experience is not isolated. Multiple mages have reported structured input during the same incursion window. I am attempting to gather accounts. Your identity will remain confidential unless you authorize otherwise.*

Sent.

She didn't respond to the anonymous voice message. There was no return address. But she saved it. Moved it from the message queue to her personal archive — the same archive she used for stream assets and contract drafts and the folder labeled MISC that contained nothing miscellaneous and everything she didn't want to file honestly.

Then she opened Priya's private message. Read it again.

*I know you saw my message three weeks ago. I know you felt it too.*

She started typing. Stopped. Her fingers hovered over nothing — the interface was neural, the typing was a metaphor, a phantom habit from before the ocular implant made physical keyboards obsolete for anything except streaming aesthetics and personal taste. But the fingers still moved when she was thinking. Still found the shapes. Still pressed silent chords into whatever surface was nearest.

She typed:

*Yeah. I felt it.*

Three words. Not four. She'd edited one out — the *too* felt like too much, felt like confirmation of something she wasn't ready to confirm, felt like joining rather than acknowledging. *I felt it* was a statement. *I felt it too* was solidarity. She wasn't ready for solidarity. She was ready for three words and a period.

She sent it.

The quiet room held. The Lumina held. The hum held its tighter note in her spine and she sat in the streaming chair she'd migrated to without noticing — the couch was for collapsing, the chair was for doing things, and sending four messages was doing something even if the something was small and insufficient and late.

She should turn off the ring light. She didn't.

She pulled up the Academy health bulletin on her HUD. Read it in full. "Structured auditory phenomena are artifacts of implant resonance feedback, not external communication. Mages experiencing persistent or unusual auditory events should consult their assigned Academy health liaison. Self-diagnosis is not recommended. Peer discussion of unverified phenomena may contribute to anticipatory anxiety and is discouraged under Section 14.3 of the Academy Communications Policy."

*Peer discussion of unverified phenomena is discouraged.*

She read that line three times. Then she closed the bulletin and opened the four messages again — Ren, Lena, Yuki, the anonymous voice — and read them side by side and the tightness in her spine matched the tightness in her chest and neither of them was resonance feedback and neither of them was something she could name.

She didn't know what it was. She wasn't going to pretend she did. But mages across multiple programs had felt the same structure during the same event and the Academy's response was a health bulletin that said *stop talking to each other* and that was an answer to a question nobody had asked yet, which meant someone, somewhere, had already asked it and been told to stop.

She touched the back of her neck. The hum. The tightness. The chord that was resolving toward something she couldn't hear.

She wasn't going to figure it out tonight.

She saved the messages. All of them. Moved them to the archive folder — the real one, not MISC, the one she'd started the night Priya's timestamp matched her scream and she'd closed the chat and taken the bump instead of thinking about it. It had been empty for three weeks. It wasn't empty now.

She turned off the ring light.

The apartment went dark except for the pink glow of her left eye — the implant, the HUD, the interface that never turned off. She sat in the chair and the hum sat in her spine and outside the window the Bay was dark and the conduits beneath the streets hummed at frequencies she could feel through the building, through the floor, through the architecture of her skeleton into the place where the R3 sat against the bone and carried a signal that was not resonance feedback and was not random and was not something she could ignore anymore even though she was going to try.

She was going to try.

The quiet room was still quiet. The forty milligrams was holding. She was in control. She was almost certain she was in control.

She closed her eyes. The hum held. Tighter now. Waiting.nn---
