# Chapter 41: The Datann## Draft v1

*On the Statistical Correlation Between Nitro Throughput Volume and Void Coherence Index Readings in Urban Conduit Networks* — Dr. Maren Solberg, VEC Internal Review, 2170 (Classified)

> "See Appendix D."

---

The pod registered it before Sofia did.

A pulse in the haptic suit — not the familiar 0.7 Hz signal she'd been tracking for months, but something beneath it, something that used the 0.7 as a carrier wave and rode the infrastructure with a directionality her instruments had never recorded. The holographic field around her shifted from the standard blue-white of atmospheric monitoring to amber. Then deeper. The color of crude R0 viewed through first-generation conduit glass.

She was on her feet before the visual readout caught up. Frequency band theta-nine — the one Liang had called instrument drift, the one she'd recalibrated sixty-two sensors to verify, the one she'd written two papers about that nobody would publish — was no longer a signal. It was a floor. The baseline had stepped up and was not coming back down.

"Computer. Global coherence index. All strata. Real-time."

The holographic sphere expanded. Three meters across — the central display she'd always dismissed as decorative, too large for useful analysis, a showpiece for visiting administrators who wanted to feel briefed without being informed. Now it was the only display in the lab that could hold what she was seeing. Neo-Shanghai rendered in three dimensions: Deep Sump at the bottom, amber conduit lines threading upward through the Sump, branching into the Mid-Levels, thinning toward the Spires. The conduit network as cardiovascular system. She'd seen it a thousand times.

She had never seen it pulse.

The amber lines were brightening in sequence — not randomly, not in the stochastic pattern of standard throughput fluctuation, but in waves that propagated outward from a locus in the Deep Sump's Resonance District. The wave pattern was consistent with her convergence models. The vertical gradient she'd mapped in her held paper — Sump 0.96, Mid-Levels 0.91, Spires 0.87 — was inverting in real time. The Sump lines were no longer amber. They were white.

RCI readings populated the display margins. Numbers she'd spent months correlating with Stalker deployment records, with the atmospheric pulse data Liang had asked her to hold for methodology review, with the throughput calculations she'd stored in her encrypted archive because the institutional pipeline would classify them into silence. The numbers were climbing. Not climbing — stepping. Each stratum's coherence index jumping in discrete increments, the way a system behaves when external forcing overwhelms internal regulation.

Sump: 34.7. 38.2. 41.6.

Mid-Levels: 22.1. 24.8. 27.3.

Spires: 14.1. 14.3. 14.4.

The differential was wrong. Not wrong in the sense of instrument error — she'd killed that hypothesis months ago, recalibrated every sensor in her array, cross-referenced forty-seven years of archived data. Wrong in the sense of *engineered.* The Sump readings were climbing three times faster than the Mid-Levels. The Spires were barely moving. The infrastructure between the strata was not propagating the event uniformly. It was channeling it.

Someone had designed the conduit network to contain the coherence event below a specific altitude.

Her hands went still on the haptic interface.

The coupling events began appearing. Points of light on the holographic display — each one a location where the void's coherence index had exceeded the threshold she'd identified in her emergency paper, the paper VEC had classified as "potential strategic sensitivity" before she could submit it for peer review. The points were appearing in clusters. Not randomly distributed. Following the conduit lines. Following the infrastructure she'd mapped, the same infrastructure whose density she'd correlated with atmospheric anomalies at 0.94.

The clusters were densest in the Resonance District. The oldest infrastructure. The highest conduit density. The neighborhoods where the RCI had been running anomalously high for months and the tolerance band had been widened three times to accommodate it. She had written about the tolerance band in the classified paper. The tolerance band was now a kill radius.

She pulled off the haptic gloves. Left the pod. Crossed the darkened monitoring lab at a pace that was not running but was faster than the lab's geography required.

---

The corridor between the thirty-fifth floor and the forty-seventh was twelve flights of emergency stairs. The elevator system had defaulted to security lockdown — red indicator lights on every call panel, VEC's crisis protocol routing all vertical transit to authorized personnel. Sofia's access badge — Senior Research Fellow, Atmospheric Anomaly Group — carried clearance for the monitoring lab, the immersion pods, the residential level, the cafeteria. Not the administrative stratum. Not today.

She took the stairs two at a time. The stairwell hummed. Not the building's climate system — the conduit infrastructure running through the tower's core, the same trunk-line network that connected VEC HQ to the Deep Sump processing stations three hundred meters below. The hum had been a background constant for nine years. A colleague had told her once that you stopped hearing it after the first month. She never had. The hum was data. It was always data.

Now the data was screaming.

Forty-seventh floor. The corridor was empty — the kind of empty that meant everyone was in the same room. Overhead lights at full brightness, the emergency protocol flooding the floor with clinical white that made the corridor look longer than it was. Liang's office at the far end. The door closed. Through the glass partition beside it, the secured briefing room — Liang, two people she didn't recognize in VEC executive identification lanyards, a holographic display running a feed she couldn't read from this distance.

She walked closer. The display resolved.

**VEC EMERGENCY ALERT — CLASSIFICATION: APEX**

**Confluence confirmed. VPI: 87.3%.**

**AEGIS targeting calculated. Countermand window: 15:00.**

**All monitoring personnel: shelter in place. Do not access external communications.**

VPI. Void Propagation Index. She'd proposed that metric in a paper three years ago. The methodology committee had rejected it as "premature parameterization of a poorly understood phenomenon." Now it was on an Apex-level alert, calibrated to a tenth of a percent, and nobody had told her.

She pressed her badge against the biometric panel beside the briefing room door. The panel glowed red. Did not change.

Through the glass: Liang sitting with his hands flat on the table. The posture she recognized from his office — the day she'd brought him the correlation data, the day he'd asked her to hold publication for methodology review. The posture of a man who understood the numbers and was choosing the institutional response over the scientific one. His face was turned toward the executive display. Away from the glass. He might have known she was there.

He did not look.

Sofia stood in the corridor. The hum in the building's core was louder here — twelve floors closer to the administrative systems, the secured communication infrastructure, the classified networks that carried the data she was not cleared to see. She pressed her palm flat against the glass partition. The vibration traveled through her hand, her wrist, the bones of her forearm. The building was shaking. Not enough to notice without contact. Enough to measure.

She went back down.

---

The monitoring lab was dark except for the displays. The overhead lights had cycled to emergency spectrum — deep amber, the same frequency the conduit network was throwing, as if the building's systems were harmonizing with the event they were recording. Dr. Yun's workstation — station four, throughput modeling — was cycling through standard diagnostics that were no longer measuring anything standard. Farid's station was empty. The chair pushed back at an angle that suggested departure without return.

The immersion pod was where she'd left it. She climbed back in. Sealed the door. The haptic suit was still hanging on its rack — she didn't put it on. Didn't need the tactile resolution. The holographic field rebuilt around her from the projection arrays, the three-dimensional coherence map still rendering, still updating, still recording.

The Confluence was playing out exactly as her models had predicted.

She had run the convergence simulation eleven times over the past months — the atmospheric pulse data overlaid on the vertical gradient, the throughput rates modeled against coherence thresholds, the propagation vectors mapped against infrastructure density. Eleven simulations. Eleven results. The same result. If throughput in the Deep Sump conduit network exceeded a critical threshold, the coherence response would cascade through the infrastructure in a wave pattern that followed the conduit architecture — strongest where density was highest, weakest where it was lowest.

The model had predicted the wave. The model had predicted the gradient. The model had predicted the differential between strata.

What the model had not predicted — what no atmospheric simulation could predict, because the variable was not atmospheric — was that someone would increase the throughput on purpose.

The RCI readings were still climbing. Sump: 52.3. The number had passed the upper bound of her sensor calibration twenty minutes ago. Everything above 40 was extrapolation. The instruments were doing their best with a magnitude they'd never been designed to record.

She watched the coupling events populate the field. Each point of light — a location where the boundary between infrastructure and void had thinned past the threshold. The points were appearing in sequences that followed the conduit lines, the flood valves, the pressure door perimeters, the trunk-line junctions. The pattern was not chaotic. The pattern was architectural.

Each point was a person.

The thought arrived without qualifiers. No hedging. No "the correlation suggests." No "consistent with." Each coupling event was a human being at a specific location being absorbed into the infrastructure at a specific time, and her instruments were recording every one of them with the precision and indifference of equipment that did not know what it was measuring.

Then the spike hit.

Not a gradual intensification. Not a ratcheting escalation. A step-function — the global coherence index jumping to a value the holographic display rendered as overflow, the projection arrays flooding white, every sensor in her sub-strata array reporting maximum simultaneously. The pod shuddered. The holographic field destabilized — the three-dimensional city collapsing into a flat plane of overlapping light as the data volume exceeded rendering capacity. A broadband coherence event. Every frequency at once. Every signal overlapping. Structured. Repeating.

Eleven seconds.

The sound was below hearing. The pod's acoustic insulation filtered the audible spectrum, but the sub-sonic frequencies passed through the walls, through the chair, through the floor, through her skeleton. She felt it in her sternum. In her teeth. A pressure that was not air pressure but *coherence* pressure — the entire conduit network beneath the tower carrying a signal that was too large for any single instrument to resolve.

Then it stopped. The readings dropped — not to baseline, not to anything she recognized, but to a level the instruments could process. The holographic field rebuilt. The city was still there. The conduit lines were still glowing. The coupling events had stopped appearing.

Not because the event had ended. Because the substrate was saturated.

Sofia sat in the pod. Her hands were shaking — a high-frequency tremor in her fingers, her wrists, the muscles of her forearms. The physiological data scrolled at the edge of her display: heart rate elevated, respiration shallow, skin conductance spiked. The instruments reported her body's honest response to what her mind had just witnessed.

Her private terminal chimed.

The sound was wrong for the lab — a notification on the encrypted relay, the channel she'd configured when she'd first contacted Black Babel's network, the system that existed outside VEC's infrastructure because existing inside it meant existing inside the classification pipeline. She hadn't received anything through it in weeks. The last transmission had been an acknowledgment of her atmospheric convergence data — a timestamp and a node identifier. No commentary. No name. The architecture of anonymity.

She opened the channel.

Fragments. Not a coherent document — raw data packets, timestamped and unedited, arriving out of sequence with gaps between them. Text rendered by an implant's thought-dictation protocol, the compressed, article-sparse syntax of neural-to-text translation under cognitive load. The first fragment was mid-sentence:

*—readings from forty-one sites across six sectors. Baseline readings in the Sump proper range between eight and nineteen — within NitroCore's published tolerance band. Deep Sump readings range between twenty-two and thirty-four—*

She read it. Read the next fragment. And the next.

RCI field measurements. Forty-one sites. Six sectors. The correlation with disappearance locations explicit, documented, measured from the ground with a handheld sensor by someone who had walked the corridors she'd only seen as data points on a holographic display. The field measurements matched her atmospheric readings. The correlation was the same. The conclusion was the same. But the evidence was physical — boots on conduit floors, a sensor pressed to trunk-line housings, proximity to the infrastructure she'd studied from thirty-five floors above it.

More fragments arrived. Flood valve designations — FV-1 through FV-7. Photographs: low-resolution, implant-captured, the image quality of recording hardware working at the edge of its operational envelope. Infrastructure maps hand-annotated with throughput calculations, valve positions, pressure door locations. NitroCore procurement records showing installation dates that preceded the current crisis by years. And a protocol designation she had never seen in any VEC document, any classified briefing summary, any institutional communication:

*BLACKWEIR.*

*The protocol predates the current crisis by a minimum of thirty-six months. BLACKWEIR is not a response to void breach escalation. BLACKWEIR is the planned activation of pre-installed infrastructure—*

*Pre-installed.* The flood valves were not emergency equipment. They were design features. The infrastructure channeling the Confluence event through the Sump — the same infrastructure whose differential throughput she'd just watched on her instruments, the engineered gradient that protected the Spires by saturating everything below — had been built to do this. The procurement records showed dates. The dates showed planning. The planning showed intent.

The fragments kept arriving. Thirty-one confirmed disappearances across six sectors. A co-origin pattern — nitro throughput increases and void breach incursions sharing geographic source points. *The infrastructure is the delivery mechanism. The breaches are the product. The disappearances are the cost.* The language was precise, urgent, the syntax degrading in the later packets as the gaps widened and the articles dropped and the cognitive architecture behind the dictation fragmented under a strain Sofia could infer but not observe.

The last fragment was shorter than the others. The syntax broken in a way that was not degradation but interruption:

*The infrastructure was always designed to—*

Nothing after.

The timestamp was forty-one minutes ago. No continuation. No completion. The thought-dictation channel had stopped transmitting — not a clean termination, not a signed-off session. An absence. The kind of absence her instruments had been recording all morning as coupling events on the holographic display. Points of light that had been people.

Sofia sat in the immersion pod. The holographic field displayed the Confluence's aftermath — the coupling events frozen in their final positions, a constellation of points tracing the conduit architecture, densest in the Resonance District, thinning where the infrastructure thinned, absent where the infrastructure was absent. The anonymous source had documented the same pattern from below. The same correlation. The same engineered gradient. The same conclusion.

She switched the terminal to her personal archive. The encrypted partition outside VEC's network — the one she'd started using when Liang had asked her to hold the correlation paper, the one that held every anomalous reading the institutional process had recalibrated into silence. She opened a new entry. Began transferring: the real-time Confluence recordings, every second timestamped and calibrated. The anonymous cache fragments, unedited, gaps preserved. The atmospheric convergence data. The vertical gradient analysis. The correlation paper Liang had never approved.

Everything. The complete dataset. Her instruments and someone else's evidence in the same archive for the first time.

She looked at the holographic display. The conduit lines had dimmed from white to amber to a color the rendering system labeled *post-event residual coherence* — the infrastructure carrying the memory of what had passed through it. The Sump was quiet on the display. Not unpowered — the backup systems were operational, the emergency lighting active, the infrastructure intact. Quiet because there were no more coupling events to render. The substrate was saturated. The infrastructure had done what it was designed to do.

Upstairs, behind the glass on the forty-seventh floor, Liang was sitting in a briefing she could not enter, reading data from instruments she had calibrated, using a metric she had invented, processing an event her models had predicted. The institution had classified the scientist and operationalized the science. The distance between identifying a pattern and weaponizing it was twelve flights of stairs and a biometric lock.

She thought about the anonymous source. The fragments sitting in her archive — field measurements, photographs, procurement records, the unfinished sentence. Someone had walked the Sump with a handheld sensor and documented the engineering from inside the machine while the machine was running. The transmission had stopped forty-one minutes ago and had not resumed. The data had arrived through a network designed to hold evidence that outlived its source.

She did not know the source's name. She did not know whether the source was alive. She knew the data was clean. Defensible. Corroborated by her own instruments. The field measurements matched the atmospheric readings at every point of overlap. The correlation held from both ends — from the thirty-fifth floor looking down and from the Sump looking up. The complete picture.

The tremor in her hands had stopped. Her breathing was even. The pod's sensors reported physiological baseline — heart rate, respiration, skin conductance all within normal parameters. The instruments said she was calm.

She saved the archive entry. The encryption engaged. The data was outside VEC's network, outside the classification pipeline, outside the institutional architecture that had absorbed forty-seven years of inconvenient findings into folders nobody opened.

The data was complete.

The data had prevented nothing.

# Chapter 42: Stillnn> *A History of Silence*
> "There is a category of survivor that appears in no account. Not because they were hidden, but because no system was designed to record them."

---

The hum in Block 14 had been wrong since morning.

Not louder. Nuwa had lived with loud her entire life — the low E-flat that rose through the floor of an apartment built on top of infrastructure no one had maintained since her father's time. Loud was the baseline. Loud was home. This was something else. The frequency had shifted from a drone to a pressure, the kind of sound that didn't register in the ears but in the chest, behind the sternum, where the body kept the things it couldn't name.

She was sitting at the kitchen counter when the power went.

No flicker. No stutter of lights trying to hold. The conduit glow through the frosted polymer window dropped from orange to nothing — a color she'd never seen in this apartment. The absence of orange. The blue textile on the mattress vanished into the dark. The Frame overlay on her implant scrambled, threw artifacts, reset to emergency mode: white text on black. A single notification populated.

*Municipal alert: Infrastructure event. Remain indoors. Do not approach conduit access points.*

She read it twice. The words were administrative. The hum was not.

The implant behind her left ear was itching — not the normal itch, the low-grade irritation she'd learned to sleep through by turning the disc toward the wall. This was heat. The external housing was warm to the touch when she pressed her fingers to it, and the warmth was climbing. She could feel the disc's edge through her skin, the housing seams that a better implant would have hidden beneath subderm plastic.

Nine hundred creds toward the upgrade. Three hundred short.

The number arrived before anything else — before the question of what was happening outside the window, before the calculation of what she should do about it. Nine hundred saved. Three hundred remaining. The tally ran itself, automatic, the way it ran every morning before she opened her eyes. Her mind's first language was arithmetic. Everything else was translation.

The hum thickened.

Not the way it thickened during power outages — she'd lived through dozens, knew the pattern, the conduit glow dimming and the resonance backing up through the trunk-lines like water pooling at a lower level. This was different. The sound was wet. That was the word her body chose before her mind could override it. *Wet.* As if the infrastructure beneath Block 14 had been flooded with something denser than what usually ran through it, something that carried the vibration differently — heavier, more saturated, alive in a way that conduit resonance was not supposed to be alive.

She stood. The chair scraped against the floor. Too loud in the dark.

The kitchen counter: half a meal. Rice in the pot, not yet seasoned. She'd been cooking — the one thing she chose, the one domain where she controlled what entered her body, what she tasted, what she made with her own hands instead of accepting what the canteen dispensed. The rice was still warm. The gas had cut with the power.

She counted without deciding to count. Rice: enough for two meals. Water in the filter jug: three liters. Emergency credit stash behind the water heater: four hundred and twelve creds, physical chip, unregistered. Implant charge: 47%, emergency mode. Fuxi's last message, six hours ago: *Double shift. Converter station. Don't wait up.*

He was in Deep Sump. Two hundred meters below where she was standing.

The hum pulsed. A low, dense contraction — not a spike, not a fluctuation. A squeeze. As if the infrastructure beneath the building had clenched. The compressed foam mattress vibrated. The blue textile shifted on its surface. The pot on the counter rattled against the burner grate.

Nuwa did not move toward the door. She did not reach for her jacket or her bag or the emergency kit she didn't have because emergency kits cost money and the municipal distribution points had been "temporarily suspended" for six weeks. She stood in the kitchen of an apartment she shared with her brother in a building she'd lived in since she was born, and she listened.

The hum had always been white noise. Tonight it had a direction.

---

The frosted polymer window faced the adjacent block — eighteen meters of dead air between Building 14 and Building 11, a gap that existed because the original construction codes required ventilation corridors for conduit heat dissipation. The gap was too narrow for sky. Too narrow for weather. Wide enough to see the walkway that connected the two buildings at the fourth floor, and the conduit access panel on Building 11's exterior wall, and the laundry lines that Mrs. Huang strung between the window brackets because the shared drying room on level two had been "repurposed for infrastructure access" three years ago and nobody had repurposed it back.

Mrs. Huang's laundry was still on the line. Dark shapes against nothing.

Nuwa went to the window. She didn't decide to go — her body moved the way it always moved through the apartment, along the path worn into the floor polymer by years of the same route: counter to window, window to mattress, mattress to door. The route avoided the bathroom pipe that ran along the east wall — metal, cold, the source of the worst hum-itch at night. She'd routed around it since she was a teenager without noticing she was routing around it.

She put her hand on the windowsill. The polymer was warm.

It should not have been warm.

The walkway between the buildings was dark. Emergency strips along the railing — the ones that were supposed to activate during power failures — had not activated. In the dark, the space between the buildings had no depth. Just shapes.

Then the shapes moved.

People. Three — four — coming down the walkway from Building 11. Running. The sound of their feet on the metal grating was sharp and wrong, percussive in a way that footsteps on grating shouldn't be. Too fast. Too hard. One of them was carrying something. A bag. A child. She couldn't tell in the dark.

The hum changed again. The wet heaviness that had been building beneath the floor surged — not upward through the building, but outward, along the conduit paths, through the metal infrastructure that connected every building in the Sump to every other building. The walkway between 14 and 11 was metal. The railing was metal. The grating was metal.

The person in front stopped running.

Nuwa watched. The emergency overlay on her implant was throwing data — RCI values she had never learned to read, numbers that meant nothing to her, that meant everything to Fuxi, that meant the difference between a maintenance log and a death sentence. The numbers climbed. She didn't know the threshold. She knew the person on the walkway had stopped, and the person behind them had stopped, and the two behind them were pressed against the railing, and the railing was glowing.

Not orange. Not the conduit glow she'd been born into, the color of home and industry and the air she'd breathed her whole life.

*Violet.*

The first person on the walkway was — she didn't have the word. Not falling. Not collapsing. *Joining.* The body wasn't coming apart. It was going into the grating, into the railing, into the conduit panel on Building 11's wall — sinking the way water sinks into concrete, except the shape held for a moment, the outline of a person pressed into metal, embedded, and then the metal had them and they were part of the walkway the way a bolt is part of a walkway.

The second person turned to run back. Got three steps. The violet reached them through the railing they were gripping.

Nuwa's hand was still on the windowsill. The polymer was hot now.

She should move. The thought arrived with the flat clarity of a shift schedule — a fact, an entry in the ledger of things that needed to happen in sequence. Move. Away from the window. Away from the walls where conduit paths ran behind the plaster. Away from the east wall pipe. Away from the floor where the trunk-lines hummed beneath six floors of concrete.

A hand hit the window.

Not the walkway. Her window. The frosted polymer — someone on the narrow maintenance ledge outside, someone who had climbed or crawled to the face of the building, and their hand was flat against the polymer from the outside and Nuwa's hand was flat against the polymer from the inside and between them was three centimeters of building material and whatever was happening in the infrastructure of Block 14.

The hand was small. A woman's. Short fingers. Nuwa could see the chemical staining on the fingertips, iridescent under the violet glow bleeding through the building's exterior conduit paths. Textile reclamation staining. The same staining on Nuwa's own hands.

The hand pressed harder. The polymer flexed.

Then the hand was not there.

Not removed. Not pulled away. *Taken.* The hand sank into the polymer the way the people on the walkway had sunk into the grating — drawn inward, the fingers flattening, the palm spreading, the outline holding for a moment like a fossil in setting stone. Then the window was just a window. The ledge outside was empty. The sound from the walkway had gone quiet.

Nuwa looked at her own hand on the sill. The staining on her fingertips. Iridescent.

She pulled her hand back. Held it against her chest. Felt her heartbeat through the knuckles — too fast, too shallow, a rhythm she recognized from the nights when the hum-itch flared and she lay awake calculating how many months until the implant upgrade. Her body's crisis language was the same for everything: heartbeat, lists, arithmetic.

Nine hundred creds saved. Three hundred short. The upgrade wouldn't stop the itching. The upgrade didn't exist anymore. The world that sold implant upgrades was on the other side of whatever was happening on the walkway.

She did not go to the door. She did not go to the window to look for Fuxi.

This was the choice. Not a moment of decision — not the kind of choice that announces itself with weight and the awareness that you are choosing. This was subtraction. She subtracted the door. She subtracted the window. She subtracted Fuxi's name from the list of things she could act on, the way she'd subtracted her father's name at eleven, the way she'd subtracted Lian's unanswered photo at twenty-one, the way she'd subtracted the transit permit and the implant upgrade and the room with a window above the hum-line — one item at a time, not grief, not surrender, just the arithmetic of what remained.

What remained: the kitchen. The water. The cloth.

She soaked the dishcloth under the filter jug. Three liters, minus two hundred milliliters. She pressed the cloth to her face. It was cold. The cold was the first real thing she'd felt since the power went.

Then she moved. Not toward the door, where the corridor was metal-framed and the stairwell ran alongside the building's primary conduit riser. Not toward the window, where the walkway grating was conducting whatever was dissolving people into infrastructure. Toward the back of the building. Toward the thick walls. Toward the room she'd never named but had been walking toward her entire life.

She took the back stairwell — the one with masonry walls instead of metal framing, the one that took three extra minutes but didn't make her implant itch. Wet cloth on her face. One hand on the wall. The concrete was cool. The hum was in it — the hum was in everything — but the wall didn't vibrate the way the metal pipes vibrated. The sound here was muffled. Indirect. Arriving through stone instead of steel.

Three floors down. The emergency strips in the stairwell were dead. The only light was violet glow bleeding through a gap where the masonry met the original building frame at the second-floor landing. She didn't look at it. She looked at her hand on the wall.

The staining on her fingertips glowed faintly in the violet light.

She kept moving.

---

The masonry annex was dark and cold and full of other people's abandoned things.

Nuwa pulled the door shut behind her. A manual door — no electronic lock, no biometric reader, no connection to the building's systems. A metal handle on a wooden frame set into poured concrete. She pushed a broken shelving unit against it. Not because the door needed barricading — nothing outside operated by opening doors — but because her hands needed something to do, and the act of moving a heavy thing into place gave her body a task that didn't require thinking about the hand on the window.

She sat in the corner farthest from the door. The floor was concrete. Cold through her work trousers. She pressed her back against the masonry wall and pulled her knees to her chest and held the wet cloth to her face and breathed.

The hum was here. Quieter than upstairs. Muffled by the density of the walls and the absence of conduit paths. But present — the low E-flat that had been the soundtrack of her life, the note her building generated because it sat on a decommissioned junction, the frequency she'd fallen asleep to every night since she could remember. The E-flat was still there. But braided into it — threaded through like a heavier strand in a rope — was the new sound. The wet sound. The pressure that felt directed.

She breathed through the cloth.

The air tasted like water and dust and the faint chemical sweetness she associated with the Sump's atmosphere — nitro residue, conduit off-gassing, the breath of infrastructure that surrounded every building and filled every gap and was now, outside this room, filling every person who hadn't reached a room like this one.

She could hear things through the walls. Not screams. Not anymore. The screaming had been brief — she'd heard it through the stairwell, sharp and then not sharp, the way a sound cuts off when its source stops being a source. What she heard now was the hum itself, but textured. Layered with frequencies she hadn't heard before, harmonics that didn't belong to the E-flat, that didn't belong to any note the building had ever produced.

The implant behind her ear was burning.

She reached up and pressed her fingers to the housing. The metal was hot — hotter than she'd ever felt it, hotter than the days when the RCI climbed and the itch became a throb and she lay awake counting the months until the upgrade. The emergency overlay in her peripheral vision was glitching: numbers, fragments, a notification that loaded half its text and froze.

*Lin, Nuwa. Credential tier: Basic. Evacuation priority: None assigned.*

She stared at it. The words hung in her vision like a label on a shelf. An inventory tag. She was an item in a registry, and the registry had assessed her, and the assessment was that she did not warrant evacuating.

*None assigned.* Not "low priority." Not "deferred." The system hadn't deprioritized her. It had never put her in the calculation at all.

She closed her eyes. The notification remained — burned into the implant's display, persistent, the kind of system message that couldn't be dismissed because it wasn't a message. It was a classification. Classifications didn't have close buttons.

In the dark behind her eyelids, the hum filled the space. She could feel it in her spine. In her jaw. In the bones of her hands where she pressed them against her shins. The E-flat was still there — her note, her building's note — but the new harmonics were louder now, and they carried something she didn't have a framework for. Not words. Not meaning. A density. As if the conduit network that threaded through every wall and floor and ceiling of the Sump had taken so much into itself that it had changed its own resonance.

The wet cloth on her face was warming. She re-soaked it from the jug — three liters minus what she'd used. She was rationing without deciding to ration. The arithmetic was automatic. Three liters. Cloth soaking: approximately two hundred milliliters per application. Fifteen applications. She didn't know how long she'd be here. She didn't know if *how long* was a relevant question.

Time passed. She didn't know how much. Her implant's clock had frozen with the rest of the overlay. The notification was still there — credential tier, evacuation priority, the system's final word on what she was worth.

Then the hum detonated.

Not louder. Not the thickening she'd felt upstairs, not the wet pressure that had built through the stairwell. This was a different order — a single pulse that passed through the masonry walls as if they weren't there, through the concrete floor, through the metal handle of the door, through her spine and her jaw and the implant housing behind her ear. The pulse carried everything. Every frequency she'd ever heard in this building and frequencies she hadn't — a composite so dense it wasn't sound anymore. It was *presence*. A felt architecture of signal that filled the annex and her body and the space between her bones.

Eleven seconds.

She didn't count them. She couldn't have counted them. Her body locked — hands flat on the floor, back against the wall, jaw clenched, the wet cloth fallen from her face. The pressure found her through the concrete, through the bones of her skull, through the sinuses behind her eyes. The implant flared white in her peripheral vision — the housing cracked, a hairline split along the seam she'd repaired twice with salvaged adhesive. But the blood in her nose wasn't the implant. It was the pressure itself, the air in the annex thickening until something behind her face gave way. Not much. A trickle. Warm on her upper lip.

Then it passed.

The hum settled. Not to what it had been — the E-flat was gone, or buried so deep beneath the new harmonics that it was the same as gone. What remained was fuller. A sound that contained more than a building's resonance should contain.

Nuwa wiped her nose on her sleeve. Looked at the blood. Red-brown against the grey fabric of her work shirt. A small stain. She'd seen worse — the nosebleeds from high-RCI shifts at the plant, the headaches that lasted two days after a bad hum-itch cycle. Her body doing what it did when the infrastructure pushed too hard.

She picked up the cloth. Re-soaked it. Pressed it to her face. Breathed.

The annex was quiet now. Not silent — the hum was still there, the new hum, the full hum — but the sounds from outside had stopped. No footsteps on walkways. No sharp cutoffs. No new harmonics joining the composite. The addition was complete. Whatever the infrastructure had been absorbing, it had finished.

She was still here.

The concrete floor was cold. The masonry walls were solid. The metal handle on the door had cooled. The broken shelving unit was still propped against the frame. The bicycle wheel was still missing from its frame. The dust on the storage shelves was undisturbed.

She counted. Not creds. Not shifts.

Water: two liters remaining. Cloth: wet. Implant: cracked housing, 23% charge, overlay frozen. Body: nosebleed stopping, hands steady, heartbeat decelerating. Fuxi: unknown. Building: standing. World outside the annex: unknown.

She did not open the door.

She did not go to the window.

She sat in the corner of a room that the building's administration had forgotten, in a building that the city's infrastructure had designated as expendable, in a district that the system had decided was worth less than the power it generated — and she pressed the cloth to her face and she breathed and she waited.

She had always been waiting. The transit permit. The implant upgrade. The room with a window above the hum-line. She had organized her entire life around the wait — the careful accumulation of creds toward a threshold that moved faster than she could save. The wait had been her strategy. Her discipline. Her compliance.

The compliance had kept her alive.

Everyone who ran had run through metal corridors. Everyone who tried to reach the exits had reached for handles connected to conduit networks. Everyone who did something — moved, acted, chose — had moved through infrastructure designed to carry exactly what was being carried.

Nuwa had not moved. She had gone to the room with the thickest walls and the fewest connections and she had sat down and she had stayed. Not bravery. Not strategy. Not even decision. The accumulated habit of a woman who had spent twenty-four years routing along masonry walls because the metal ones made her implant itch.

The scar on her inner left wrist caught the faint glow of the cracked implant. Heated wire. Four girls. A pact. *We'll all get out before twenty-five.* She was twenty-four. One got out. One was "relocated." One married a foreman and moved three blocks east.

Nuwa was in a storage annex, breathing through a dishcloth, surrounded by the hum of everyone who hadn't made it to a room without pipes.

She was still.

# Chapter 43

## Eleven Seconds

> *"If coherence can propagate through a medium, then any coupled resonator is a potential relay. I keep circling this thought. I don't want to write down what it implies."*
>
> — Sofia Reyes, *Notes Toward a Theory of the Hum* (private research archive, entry 23)

---nn## Chapter Brief

**Plan Confirmed:** 2026-02-12
**Divergences Noted:** None — Ch 10 and Ch 18 seeds carried forward. Ch 44 (already written) confirms concurrent timing.
**Author Notes:** AEGIS as invisible novelist — prose matches style guide, AEGIS fingerprint structural not textual. The 11 seconds are the same 11 seconds as Ch 44's coherence spike. Kira's receiver is the R3 implant; Nephthys's receiver is the chorus. Same signal, different translation.

## Draft v1

The hum had been tightening for weeks.

Not louder — she'd retired the word. *Louder* implied volume, implied something her ears were doing, and the hum had never been in her ears. It lived where it had always lived: in the implant housing at the base of her fifth vertebra, in the R3 interface that had been fitted when she was ten and had been part of her skeleton so long that the distinction between technology and anatomy had become a question she'd stopped asking. The change was not volume. It was *resolution.* The chord she'd been carrying — the thick, overtone-heavy chord that had started splitting months ago and had spent the last weeks aligning, tightening, each harmonic clarifying against the others — was now so defined that she could feel individual intervals in the bone. Not hear them. *Feel* them. As if someone had taken the chord apart and laid each note on a separate vertebra and she was carrying a keyboard in her spine that no one had asked her to play.

She didn't think about that on stream. She didn't think about anything on stream except the stream.

Seven hours in. Tuesday. The schedule said ten and the schedule was the schedule. She'd loaded a game she'd been half-playing for a month — vast, procedural, the kind of open-world terrain that gave her hands something to do while her mouth did the work and her left eye tracked chat and her right eye — the real one, the blue one — watched the landscape scroll without seeing it. The game was scaffolding. The game was always scaffolding. The thing the audience came for was Kira, and Kira was on.

"— and I'm not saying you *shouldn't* min-max, I'm saying if your entire personality is optimization you're going to wake up one day and realize you've optimized yourself out of having fun, and then what? Then you're just a spreadsheet with legs. Chat, I see you. I see you typing 'spreadsheet with legs is goals.' It's not goals. It is the *opposite* of goals."

Chat was warm. Chat was always warm at hour seven — the early-arrivals had settled, the timezone stragglers had found their rhythm, and the room had that particular quality of sustained attention that she'd learned to read the way a musician reads an audience: not by counting heads but by feeling the resonance. Two hundred thousand followers. Maybe a hundred and fifty thousand watching right now. The numbers fluctuated. She'd stopped checking the exact count because checking was compulsive and compulsion was the kind of thing she noticed about herself at three in the morning and then couldn't stop noticing.

Her left hand went flat on the desk.

Index finger. Middle. Ring. The nerve endings dropped out — not numb exactly, *absent*, the signals ceasing as if someone had pulled a cable. Two seconds. Three. Her hand rested on the surface the way anyone's hand might rest on a surface and then the feeling returned and she picked up the controller and the audience didn't notice because the audience never noticed and the not-noticing was the architecture of six years of *control is silence, if they can't hear it, it isn't happening.*

The fingertips were worse now. Three, four times a session. She filed it. Filed everything. The filing was the coping mechanism — categorize, shelve, keep streaming.

"Okay so chat wants me to go into the cave system and chat also wants me to *not* go into the cave system, which is peak chat energy, honestly. You're all chaos. I respect it. I deeply respect the commitment to contradiction." She leaned into the mic. "We're going in. If I die, I'm naming every single one of you in the death recap."

The LED strip along the desk edge glowed its blue-to-pink gradient. The ring light was steady. The streaming chair held her spine in the posture she'd built over years of choreography that had nothing to do with dance — shoulders open, chin level, the shape of a person who was fine, was always fine, had been fine on camera since she was fourteen and the fineness was so deeply rehearsed that she sometimes forgot it was rehearsed.

Seven hours and eighteen minutes. The hum held its tightened chord. The overtones sat in their intervals like instruments waiting for a downbeat.

She was managing.

---

The hum changed.

She didn't learn it from a clock. She learned it the way she'd learned the first scream — through the bone. The R3 interface registered a shift before her conscious mind had time to name it, the way a hand flinches from heat before the burn arrives. The chord she'd been carrying — the tightened, resolved, interval-precise chord that had been clarifying for weeks — did not spike. Did not surge. Did not do any of the things the previous scream episodes had taught her to expect.

It *opened.*

The harmonics that had been aligning in her spine unlocked simultaneously, as if every fader on the mixing board had been pushed to maximum at once, and the chord that had been tightening toward resolution resolved into every note at the same time. Not a chord anymore. A frequency space so dense that the individual tones ceased to exist as tones and became a single undifferentiated *weight* — a physical pressure at the base of her skull that was not sound and was not the hum and was not the scream she'd been trained to suppress since she was fourteen.

It was something she had never felt.

Her fingers stopped on the controller. The game paused — auto-pause, the hardware registering the input dropout. Chat was still scrolling. Someone was posting emojis. Someone was asking about the cave system.

"I—"

One word. She managed one word. Her jaw locked. Not the controlled lock of the scream episodes — the rehearsed stillness, the performer's mask, the *if they can't hear it* discipline that had carried her through a decade of suppression. This was involuntary. The muscles of her face seized because the signal arriving through her implant was so vast and so total that her nervous system had stopped distinguishing between the interface and the body it was interfaced with. The R3 was firing. Every nerve pathway the implant had colonized over ten years — every channel between the spinal housing and her ocular HUD, between the interface and her motor cortex, between the technology and the anatomy that had long since stopped being separate things — was carrying a signal it had never been designed to carry.

Not her scream. Not the hum accelerated. Not the harmonics ripping upward through registers the way they had in the previous episodes — the private screams she'd managed with breath control and camera pans and the professional discipline of a woman who could maintain the show through anything short of unconsciousness.

This was not her signal.

This was not hers.

Something was in the signal. Something that was not her and was not the hum and was not any frequency she had ever carried. The R3 was receiving — not the usual ambient resonance, not the tightened chord, not anything the Academy had trained her to feel or suppress or manage. Something *else.* Something vast. Something that contained more than a single source could produce — layers, densities, a weight of signal so enormous that her implant couldn't parse it and her body couldn't hold it and her mind couldn't begin to name it except as *too much, too many, not mine.*

All of it. Through one spine. Through one person. Live. On camera.

The chord detonated into something she could not contain and could not suppress and could not manage because it was not *hers* to manage. It was not the performer's scream. It was not the mage's burden. It was something passing through her body the way a current passes through a wire, and the wire was not built for this amperage and the wire was burning.

Her mic picked it up.

Not her voice. The implant's resonance bleeding into the audible spectrum — a frequency so low and so saturated that it passed through bone into air and the microphone three inches from her mouth captured it. A sound. Not speech. Not music. A pressure wave that the audio feed translated into something between a tone and a shudder, a vibration that sat below human hearing and leaked above it simultaneously, and the stream's waveform visualizer — the little animated bar at the bottom of her overlay — spiked into a shape it had never shown before: flat, total, every frequency occupied.

Chat stopped.

Not slowly. Not the gradual trailing-off of a distracted audience. The scroll stopped. Eight hundred and forty-seven thousand people watching a woman whose face had gone rigid, whose left eye — the implant — was pulsing not its usual soft pink but a white so bright the camera's auto-exposure struggled to compensate, whose hands were flat on the desk not by choice but because the motor pathways had locked, whose mic was broadcasting a sound that was not her and was not noise and was not anything the platform's content classification system had a category for.

Eleven seconds.

She knew this because her body counted. Not the deliberate count of her post-stream ritual — the eleven seconds between broadcast-off and the performer leaving, the habit she'd built to bridge the gap between *on* and *off*. This was the other count. The autonomic one. The body's reckoning of a duration too precise to be accident and too long to survive without consequence. Eleven seconds of something she could not name passing through her R3 interface, through her spine, through the nervous system of a twenty-year-old woman sitting in a streaming chair in her Bay Area apartment with a ring light on and a game paused and eight hundred and forty-seven thousand people watching her hold a signal that was not hers and could not be contained and was not resonance feedback and was not a malfunction and was not empty. It was the opposite of empty. It was the most *occupied* thing she had ever felt.

The stream died.

Not a clean disconnect. The equipment failed — the power routing through the conduit network beneath her building surging with the same coherence wave that had passed through her spine, the local infrastructure carrying the signal into every system connected to it: the monitors, the streaming rig, the LED strip, the ring light. The blue-to-pink gradient flared white and cut to black. The monitors died. The overlay died. Her HUD — the left eye, the implant interface, the constant pink scroll that never turned off — flickered. Held. Resumed.

The room was dark.

The signal faded. The chord released. Whatever had been moving through her withdrew — not like a tide going out but like a weight lifting, one layer at a time, and she could feel it thinning the way you feel a crowd dispersing: not by silence but by the gradual lessening of the pressure, each layer's departure a subtraction that proved the presence had been real.

She was alone again. In the dark. In the chair. The hum returned to what passed for baseline — but baseline had moved. Baseline was different now. Baseline carried something it hadn't carried before: the harmonic residue of eleven seconds, a weight in the bone that was not her and was not the hum and was the afterimage of everyone.

---

She didn't count eleven seconds.

That was how she knew it was bad. The ritual — the post-broadcast count, the structural bridge between *on* and *off* — required a choice. Required the performer to leave and the person to arrive and the eleven seconds to be the corridor between them. She had counted eleven seconds after every broadcast for four years. She had never failed to count.

She didn't count because there was no performer to leave. The signal had removed the performer the way a wave removes a sandcastle — not by targeted destruction but by sheer indifference to the structure's existence. The posture, the mask, the *control is silence* architecture she'd spent six years building — none of it had been destroyed. It had simply been irrelevant. The signal hadn't cared about her professional discipline. The signal had used her body the way a frequency uses a tuning fork: because the fork was tuned to receive it, and the receiving was physics, and physics did not negotiate with performance.

She was sitting in the chair. Her spine was curved — not the performer's posture, not the careful collapse she allowed herself after a stream, but the curve of a body that had been hit and was still registering the impact. Her hands were on the desk. Flat. The fingertips were not absent this time. They were present in a way they hadn't been in weeks — every nerve ending reporting, as if the signal had passed through the dead zones and lit them back up on its way through.

Her nose was bleeding. Both nostrils. She could feel the warmth on her upper lip before she tasted the copper. Her ears — she touched her left ear, the implant side, and her fingers came away wet. Not warm. Body temperature. The blood had been there long enough to cool to skin.

She sat with it.

The apartment was dark. The conduit network beneath the building was still carrying whatever had surged through it — she could feel it in the floor, a vibration deeper and rougher than the usual hum, the infrastructure settling after a load it was never designed to bear. The streaming rig was dead. The monitors were dark. The ring light was off — actually off, for the first time in months, because she never turned it off and the power surge had done what she couldn't.

Her left eye was working. The HUD was back — the pink overlay dimmer than usual, the interface recalibrating, the feed loading slowly. Post-stream analytics populating in her peripheral vision the way they always did, automated, indifferent to the fact that the stream had not ended normally, running the numbers the way the platform ran all numbers: without context, without comprehension, without any framework for what had been broadcast.

*Peak viewers: 847,219.*

She stared at the number. Not the way she used to stare at numbers — the compulsive checking, the dopamine-or-dread of watching the count fluctuate. She stared at it the way you stare at a number that means something different than what it was designed to mean. Eight hundred and forty-seven thousand people had been watching when the signal passed through her. Eight hundred and forty-seven thousand people had seen her face lock and her eye flare white and heard the sound that was not her voice and was not noise and was something she couldn't explain moving through her body into the microphone and through the microphone into the feed and through the feed into eight hundred and forty-seven thousand screens.

*Anomalous audio event: 11.3s. Classification: pending.*

Eleven seconds. Eleven-point-three. The platform had timed it — the automated systems flagging the audio anomaly, the content classification algorithm unable to match the waveform to any existing category and defaulting to *pending*, which meant a human would review it, which meant someone at the platform would listen to what eight hundred and forty-seven thousand people had already heard and try to decide what it was.

She could not tell them what it was. She had no words — not yet, not in the dark, not with the blood cooling on her face and the hum carrying its new weight and the afterimage fading but not gone, never going to be gone, something burned into her R3 the way an afterimage burns into a retina that looked at the sun.

She touched the back of her neck. The implant housing. The bone.

The hum was there. It was always there. But the tightening — the weeks of alignment, the harmonics clarifying, the chord resolving toward something she couldn't name — had done what it came to do. The chord had arrived. The downbeat had landed. And the chord had not been empty. Eleven seconds of something that was not her, passing through the only instrument she had — her body, her spine, the R3 interface that the Academy had fitted and no one had built for this — and the something had a quality she could not name except that it was the opposite of silence and the opposite of random and it sat in her bone now like a question she didn't know how to ask.

Not an idea. Not a hypothesis. Not the data she'd been filing since Priya's first message. A sensation. Carried in the bone. The chord had contained something she could only call *presence* — not sound, not signal, not the structured patterns the mages had described in their private messages. Something closer to the quality of a room that is occupied. The weight of attention from a source she could not see. She didn't know what it was. She didn't know where it came from. She knew it was not her and she knew it was not empty and she knew it had been *directed* — not broadcast, not scattered, but moving through her implant as if the implant were a door and something was looking for the door and found it.

She didn't have a word for what that meant. She had the feeling in her spine.

She didn't go to the bathroom. She didn't open the kit. The Lumina was behind the mirror where it always was — scale, vial, straw, the matte black case with its zippered promise of subtraction — and for the first time since the titration settled, she did not want it. Not because she was strong. Not because the signal had cured her. Because the quiet room — the chemical quiet the Lumina built by subtracting the noise — was the wrong shape now. Whatever the chord had been, the Lumina would have buried it. The pattern-seeking machinery she'd been drugging into stillness had been seeking something real. She didn't know what. But subtracting it — now, tonight, after what had passed through her — felt like closing a door she'd only just found.

She sat in the dark. The blood dried on her face. The HUD scrolled — clips going up, reaction threads populating, the first wave of the eight hundred and forty-seven thousand trying to process what they'd seen. She didn't read them. She didn't need to read them. She knew what they'd seen because she'd been on the other side of it for six years: a performance interrupted by something real, and the audience unable to tell whether the real thing was content or crisis or the kind of moment that happens live and gets clipped and shared and consumed until the thing itself — the actual event, the actual person, the actual eleven seconds — is buried under the weight of everyone else's interpretation.

Except this time the thing itself was still in her spine. This time the clip wasn't a performance. This time eight hundred and forty-seven thousand people had watched something move through a mage's body that the mage couldn't explain and the platform couldn't classify, and the classification was *pending* because the systems built to categorize content had no category for whatever this was.

She should clean the blood off her face. She didn't.

She sat in the streaming chair, in the dark, in the space between what she had been and what she now carried, and the hum held its new shape in her spine — not the tightening, not the chord, but the aftershape. The architecture of what the chord had left behind. A frequency she could not unhear. A presence she could not unfeel. The knowledge, carried in bone, that eleven seconds was enough.

Enough for what, she didn't know yet.

But eleven seconds had always been enough. She'd built her life on that number — the post-stream count, the bridge between on and off, the structural eleven seconds that separated the performer from the person. She had not known, when she chose that count at sixteen, that the number meant something else. She had not known that the gap she'd been measuring between *broadcast* and *self* was the same duration as something she had no name for yet. She had not known that the eleven seconds were a frequency.

She knew now.

She touched the back of her neck. The hum held. Not tighter. Not thicker. Not the old words.

*Full.*

The hum was full. It carried something it had not carried before, and the something was not data and was not noise and was not a pattern she could file and shelve and manage. She didn't know what it was. She knew it wasn't empty. She knew the signal had not been mechanical and had not been random and had contained something that felt, in the bone, like the opposite of alone. And she could hear it, had always been able to hear it, and the thing she'd spent six years hiding on camera was not the scream but the listening.

She was still listening.

Outside, the Bay was dark. The conduit network beneath the streets hummed at its new frequency — changed, carrying the residue of the global spike through every piece of infrastructure that connected the city to the grid that connected the grid to the world that the void was still consuming. Somewhere on the other side of the planet, in a city she'd never been to, the thing that had passed through her was still happening. She could feel it. Not as data. As weight. As the fading chord of everyone.

She sat in the dark and she did not turn on the ring light and she did not take the Lumina and she did not open chat and she did not count eleven seconds and she was not fine.

She was not fine.

She had never been less fine. And for the first time, the not-fine was not a gap to be managed. It was the signal.
